title: rplatypus
text:
Reads a sample of one split’s masks and reports what the specification’s colours, or list of labels, actually matched. Trains nothing and loads no model.



inspect_masks(spec, split = c("train", "validation", "test"), limit = 500)







spec


A platypus_spec().




split


“train”, “validation” or “test”.




limit


How many masks to read. They are spread across the split rather than taken from its start, because datasets arrive sorted and a prefix would answer about the beginning.






platypus_fit() does a small version of this before every run and refuses when a declared class appears in none of the masks it read. This is the same question asked deliberately, over as much of the data as you want - which is what to reach for when that refusal looks wrong.



A one-row data frame: unmatched, samples_checked, total_samples, and present_classes and missing_classes as comma-separated strings so the frame stays printable - region names where the specification gave regions, and class numbers otherwise, which is what the engine’s own refusal does. The positions are attached as integer vectors in the attributes present and missing either way, so anything reading them keeps working.



missing_classes is the one to act on. A class that appears in no mask cannot be learned: its channel of the target is zero everywhere, so there is no gradient towards it and the model is never shown the thing it is being asked to find. Either the colours do not describe these masks, or they name a class the data does not contain.
With regions the classes are named rather than numbered, because a position is the one thing a reader cannot resolve: missing_classes: 1 means the second region, and counting entries in a configuration file to find out which is the step nobody takes. The positions are still there, as the missing and present attributes.
That naming matters most for the one failure regions invites: of = 3 against a label map holding 4 is a channel of zeros, so the model trains to predict nothing and scores a Dice of 0 for that region while every other number in the run looks ordinary. The engine refuses it before training and names the region; this is how to ask the same question over more of the data than the refusal reads.
unmatched is the fraction of mask pixels matching no entry, which fall back to the background class. Read it knowing that it scales with the size of the thing being segmented, so it is loud for a large structure and almost silent for a small lesion. Measured on masks that are white, with a colormap asking for a colour that is not there: a foreground covering 20% of the image gives 19.8%, and one covering 0.6% gives 0.61% - which is less than the 0.72% that JPEG compression leaves around the edge of a perfectly correct mask. That is why the refusal is built on class presence instead.




library("rplatypus")

inspect_masks(spec)
inspect_masks(spec, split = "validation", limit = 2000)
crumbs: What the colormap or labels match in your masks

title: rplatypus
text:
Four members of the U-shaped family. They take the same arguments and differ only in what happens between the contracting and expanding paths: u_net concatenates its skip connections, linknet adds them, res_u_net makes each block residual, and u_net_plus_plus fills in the nested skip pathways.



u_net(
  name,
  input_shape,
  channels = NULL,
  n_class = NULL,
  blocks = NULL,
  filters = NULL,
  block_width = NULL,
  dropout = NULL,
  batch_normalization = NULL,
  separable_conv = NULL,
  spatial_dropout = NULL,
  upsample = NULL,
  deep_supervision = NULL,
  activation = NULL,
  initialiser = NULL,
  loss = NULL,
  metrics = NULL,
  optimizer = NULL,
  callbacks = NULL,
  augmentation = NULL,
  epochs = NULL,
  batch_size = NULL,
  splits = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  fit = NULL,
  encoder = NULL,
  pretrained = NULL,
  freeze_encoder = NULL,
  encoder_learning_rate = NULL,
  separation = NULL,
  decode = NULL
)

  input_shape,
  channels = NULL,
  n_class = NULL,

)

  name,
  input_shape,
  channels = NULL,
  n_class = NULL,
  blocks = NULL,
  filters = NULL,
  block_width = NULL,
  dropout = NULL,
  batch_normalization = NULL,
  separable_conv = NULL,
  spatial_dropout = NULL,
  upsample = NULL,

  activation = NULL,
  initialiser = NULL,

  freeze_encoder = NULL,

  decode = NULL
)

linknet(
  name,
  input_shape,
  channels = NULL,
  n_class = NULL,
  blocks = NULL,
  filters = NULL,
  block_width = NULL,
  dropout = NULL,
  batch_normalization = NULL,
  separable_conv = NULL,
  spatial_dropout = NULL,
  upsample = NULL,
  deep_supervision = NULL,
  activation = NULL,
  initialiser = NULL,
  loss = NULL,
  metrics = NULL,
  optimizer = NULL,
  callbacks = NULL,
  augmentation = NULL,
  epochs = NULL,
  batch_size = NULL,
  splits = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  fit = NULL,
  encoder = NULL,
  pretrained = NULL,
  freeze_encoder = NULL,
  encoder_learning_rate = NULL,
  separation = NULL,
  decode = NULL
)







name


Unique within a specification. It names this model’s outputs, its rows in every score table, and the directory its run record is written to - so two models called the same thing would overwrite one record and report it as two, which is why the engine refuses a repeat rather than disambiguating it.




input_shape


Tile size: c(height, width), or c(depth, height, width).




channels


Input channels. 3 for colour, 1 for greyscale. Derived from channels_from when segmentation_data() names one file per channel.




n_class


Removed. The number of classes comes from the data - colormap or labels in segmentation_data() - and a model that also declared it could only ever disagree with its own data. Passing it is an error that says so.




blocks


How many times the resolution is halved. Taken from the weights file when weights is given and this is not.




filters


Filters in the first block; doubled at each level. Taken from the weights file when weights is given and this is not.




block_width


Convolutions per block. Two is the usual U-Net block; one trains faster and holds less, three rarely pays for itself. It composes with every architecture, including the residual blocks of res_u_net(), where it is the number of convolutions inside the residual rather than beside it.




dropout


Drop this fraction of activations in every block during training, 0 to switch it off. The first thing to reach for when the training loss keeps falling and the validation loss does not.




batch_normalization


Normalise each batch’s activations between convolutions, which is what lets a deeper network train at all at a useful learning rate. On by default; the reason to turn it off is a batch so small that its statistics are noise, which is the case a 3D run with batch_size = 1 lands in.




separable_conv


Depthwise-separable convolutions. Far fewer parameters, a little slower to converge.




spatial_dropout


Drop whole feature maps rather than individual activations. On an image the neighbouring pixels of a dropped activation carry almost the same information, so ordinary dropout removes less than it appears to; dropping a channel removes a feature. Does nothing unless dropout is above 0, which sets the rate.




upsample


Interpolate and convolve instead of using a transposed convolution.




deep_supervision


Train every decoder depth, not only the last. u_net_plus_plus only, since it is the one with intermediate outputs to supervise.




activation


One of “relu”, “leaky_relu”, “elu”, “selu”, “gelu”, “silu”, “tanh”.




initialiser


One of “he_normal”, “he_uniform”, “glorot_normal”, “glorot_uniform”.




loss


The objective trained against, see losses and available_losses(). It is what a score table’s loss column is comparable within and not across: a Focal-Tversky of 0.05 is not better than a cross-entropy of 0.14, it is a different question, which is why the table carries the loss’s name beside the number. Unset uses the engine’s default.




metrics


A list of metrics, see metrics.




optimizer


An optimiser, see optimizers.




callbacks


A list of callbacks, see callbacks.




augmentation


A list of augmentation_step() steps, applied to training data only.




epochs, batch_size


Training length and batch size.




splits


Cut each image into a grid of tiles instead of shrinking it: one number per spatial dimension, so c(2, 3) gives six tiles. Use it to segment a large image without throwing away resolution; predictions are reassembled to the original size.




weights


A checkpoint to start from, or to use as-is with fit = FALSE.




fit


Set FALSE to load weights and skip training.




encoder


A pretrained-architecture backbone to use as the contracting path instead of the built-in encoder, named as timm names it: “resnet34”, “efficientnet_b0”, “mobilenetv3_large_100”, “densenet121”, “vgg16” and the other convolutional families. Naming one builds that architecture; it does not load anything. 2D only - ImageNet is images, so a backbone with a 3D input_shape is refused while the specification is read. The patch-based families (convnext_, swin_) are refused too: their features start at a quarter of the input, and the half-resolution level a U-shaped decoder recovers fine detail from does not exist. blocks then says how many of the backbone’s stages to use.




pretrained


Load the backbone’s ImageNet weights. Separate from encoder on purpose, so naming an architecture never reaches the network on a machine that has none. Measured on three datasets, transfer does not beat the built-in encoder here - see encoders for the table and what it is actually good for.




freeze_encoder


Hold the transferred layers still for this many epochs, then train them. Use this rather than encoder_learning_rate alone: it was the better of the two on all three datasets measured. A number at or above epochs keeps them fixed for the whole run.




encoder_learning_rate


A separate, smaller rate for the layers that arrived pretrained. The full-resolution stage in front of them is platypus’s own and starts random, so it keeps the optimiser’s rate. Giving this instead of freeze_encoder measured worse everywhere, and on one dataset worse than no backbone at all.




separation


What the network predicts so that touching objects can be told apart - separation_rim() or separation_flows(). Giving it is what makes this an instance model: it has no counterpart on a semantic one, so a model carrying it can only mean instances, which is how a specification knows its task without anybody typing it. The data has to be instance_data() to match. The head’s width follows from the signal and the number of classes and is derived rather than stated.
It may be left out when weights names a file that records it, since pyplatypus 0.8.0a28: a published sidecar says what the channels were trained to predict, and “dsbowl-instances” is a rim of width 2 - a training decision rather than a shape, and nothing a reader can guess from a model card. So u_net(“objects”, input_shape = c(256, 256), weights = “dsbowl-instances”) beside instance_data() is an instance model, and the engine prints what it adopted.
Left out with no weights it is still semantic, and still refused beside instance_data() as two tasks in one specification - which is the pair that would otherwise be silent: the same layout and the same architecture, differing only in whether a signal is predicted at all. maju116/rplatypus#181.




decode


A list of decodings turning those channels into objects, e.g. list(decode_nearest_seed(), decode_connected_components()). A list rather than one, because several decodings share a single forward pass: a second costs seconds where a second training run costs an hour, so evaluate() returns a row per model and decoding. Unset, the engine uses the signal’s own decoding plus decode_connected_components(), which ignores the signal and is therefore the row the others have to be read against. Only meaningful with separation.






input_shape is the tile the model sees: two numbers for images, three for volumes. Its length is what makes a model 2D or 3D - there is no separate switch. Every spatial dimension must divide by 2^blocks, or the decoder cannot line up with the encoder, and that is checked when the specification is built rather than part-way through training.



A model specification, to be passed to platypus_spec().



Every argument below except name and input_shape is NULL unless you set it, and a NULL is left out of the request entirely - so the engine’s own default applies. The defaults are therefore written down once, in pyplatypus, rather than here as well:
channels 3        blocks 4          filters 16      block_width 2
dropout 0         batch_normalization TRUE          separable_conv FALSE
spatial_dropout TRUE                upsample FALSE  deep_supervision FALSE
activation "relu"                   initialiser "he_normal"
loss cce          metrics iou       optimizer adam  callbacks none
epochs 10         batch_size 8      fit TRUE

The second reason matters more than tidiness. A value sent is indistinguishable from a value chosen, so defaults travelling from here would silence the engine’s own knowledge: weights naming a published file records its architecture, blocks and filters, and those are adopted only where the specification stayed silent. Sending blocks = 4 because that is what R happened to say would override a file that knows better.




library("rplatypus")

u_net("unet", input_shape = c(256, 256), blocks = 4, filters = 16)

$name
[1] "unet"

$architecture
[1] "u_net"

$input_shape
[1] 256 256

$blocks
[1] 4

$filters
[1] 16

# A large image, tiled rather than shrunk
u_net("hd", input_shape = c(256, 256), splits = c(4, 6))

$name
[1] "hd"

$architecture
[1] "u_net"

$input_shape
[1] 256 256

$splits
[1] 4 6

pretrained


Load the backbone’s ImageNet weights. Separate from encoder on purpose, so naming an architecture never reaches the network on a machine that has none. Measured on three datasets, transfer does not beat the built-in encoder here - see encoders for the table and what it is actually good for.




freeze_encoder


Hold the transferred layers still for this many epochs, then train them. Use this rather than encoder_learning_rate alone: it was the better of the two on all three datasets measured. A number at or above epochs keeps them fixed for the whole run.




encoder_learning_rate


A separate, smaller rate for the layers that arrived pretrained. The full-resolution stage in front of them is platypus’s own and starts random, so it keeps the optimiser’s rate. Giving this instead of freeze_encoder measured worse everywhere, and on one dataset worse than no backbone at all.




separation


What the network predicts so that touching objects can be told apart - separation_rim() or separation_flows(). Giving it is what makes this an instance model: it has no counterpart on a semantic one, so a model carrying it can only mean instances, which is how a specification knows its task without anybody typing it. The data has to be instance_data() to match. The head’s width follows from the signal and the number of classes and is derived rather than stated.
It may be left out when weights names a file that records it, since pyplatypus 0.8.0a28: a published sidecar says what the channels were trained to predict, and “dsbowl-instances” is a rim of width 2 - a training decision rather than a shape, and nothing a reader can guess from a model card. So u_net(“objects”, input_shape = c(256, 256), weights = “dsbowl-instances”) beside instance_data() is an instance model, and the engine prints what it adopted.
Left out with no weights it is still semantic, and still refused beside instance_data() as two tasks in one specification - which is the pair that would otherwise be silent: the same layout and the same architecture, differing only in whether a signal is predicted at all. maju116/rplatypus#181.




decode


A list of decodings turning those channels into objects, e.g. list(decode_nearest_seed(), decode_connected_components()). A list rather than one, because several decodings share a single forward pass: a second costs seconds where a second training run costs an hour, so evaluate() returns a row per model and decoding. Unset, the engine uses the signal’s own decoding plus decode_connected_components(), which ignores the signal and is therefore the row the others have to be read against. Only meaningful with separation.






input_shape is the tile the model sees: two numbers for images, three for volumes. Its length is what makes a model 2D or 3D - there is no separate switch. Every spatial dimension must divide by 2^blocks, or the decoder cannot line up with the encoder, and that is checked when the specification is built rather than part-way through training.



A model specification, to be passed to platypus_spec().



Every argument below except name and input_shape is NULL unless you set it, and a NULL is left out of the request entirely - so the engine’s own default applies. The defaults are therefore written down once, in pyplatypus, rather than here as well:
channels 3        blocks 4          filters 16      block_width 2
dropout 0         batch_normalization TRUE          separable_conv FALSE
spatial_dropout TRUE                upsample FALSE  deep_supervision FALSE
activation "relu"                   initialiser "he_normal"
loss cce          metrics iou       optimizer adam  callbacks none
epochs 10         batch_size 8      fit TRUE

The second reason matters more than tidiness. A value sent is indistinguishable from a value chosen, so defaults travelling from here would silence the engine’s own knowledge: weights naming a published file records its architecture, blocks and filters, and those are adopted only where the specification stayed silent. Sending blocks = 4 because that is what R happened to say would override a file that knows better.




library("rplatypus")

u_net("unet", input_shape = c(256, 256), blocks = 4, filters = 16)

$name
[1] "unet"

$architecture
[1] "u_net"

$input_shape
[1] 256 256

$blocks
[1] 4

$filters
[1] 16

# A large image, tiled rather than shrunk
u_net("hd", input_shape = c(256, 256), splits = c(4, 6))

$name
[1] "hd"

$architecture
[1] "u_net"

$input_shape
[1] 256 256

$splits
[1] 4 6

title: rplatypus
text:
Dice and IoU count a voxel the same wherever it sits, which is why a model can reach 0.88 on Dice while its volumes run a fifth too large: the overshoot is all at the boundary, and for a small lesion the boundary is most of the object. This adds mean(phi * p), where phi is the signed distance to the truth’s boundary - negative inside, positive outside - so a voxel predicted far outside the truth costs in proportion to how far.



loss_boundary(region = NULL, alpha = NULL)







region


The overlap term this is added to - any other loss. Unset uses the engine’s default, which is Dice. loss_focal() here is what this feature was originally asked for: focal combined with a distance metric. loss_generalized_dice() here is the combination worth knowing about, because the two features are motivated by the same picture: this loss exists for a lesion in a thousandth of a frame, and a surface term exists for an object whose boundary is most of it.




alpha


How much of the objective is the region term, 1 - alpha the surface term. Unset uses the engine’s default of 0.9.
Not 0.5, and that was measured. At 0.5 the surface term owns half the objective while the prediction is still random, which is where it is unstable: three seeds gave a volume error spread of ±28.28% against the baseline’s ±3.11%, with every number worse. Left unset here on purpose - the number is a measurement and belongs in the one place the measurement lives, so that an engine that learns better cannot be contradicted from this side.






What it buys and what it costs, measured. Three seeds, 60 epochs, lesions with ambiguous edges, against Dice alone:



loss


Dice


volume bias


volume |error|




loss_dice()


0.9525 ±0.0027


-5.18% ±3.11%


16.90% ±0.90%




loss_boundary()


0.9411 ±0.0093


-0.06% ±4.15%


22.17% ±2.88%



It trades accuracy per case for being unbiased over a series. "Is there a lesion" wants the overlap; "has it grown since March" wants a volume that is not systematically wrong, and no single number answers both - which is the same point mask_volume() makes about reporting millilitres beside an overlap score. The bias improvement is suggestive on three seeds, since the baseline’s own bias wanders ±3.11%; the costs are established.
It costs time too. The signed distance transform runs once per sample, in the loader’s workers: 5.3 ms for a 256x256 image, 23.4 ms for a 64x64x32 volume and 709.8 ms at 128^3. On large volumes give platypus_fit() workers, or the transform becomes the training.



A loss specification, to be passed to a model constructor.



losses for the losses that can be the region term - every one of them except the three that score numbers and this one, held to the engine’s own union by a test rather than counted here - and mask_volume() for reading a volume in millilitres rather than voxels.




library("rplatypus")

loss_boundary()

$name
[1] "boundary"

$region
NULL

$alpha
NULL

loss_boundary(region = loss_focal(gamma = 2))

$name
[1] "boundary"

$region
$region$name
[1] "focal"

$region$gamma
[1] 2

$region$alpha
NULL


$alpha
NULL

loss_boundary(region = loss_dice(), alpha = 0.95)

$name
[1] "boundary"

$region
$region$name
[1] "dice"

$region$smooth
[1] 1


$alpha
[1] 0.95

A loss that knows how far a wrong voxel is from the truth

title: rplatypus
text:
The convention optical flow has used for twenty years, and a convention rather than a palette decision - which is why it is not in drawing_style(). Nothing about it is a choice this project gets to make differently from everyone else’s figures, and a reader who has seen one flow visualisation can read this one.



flow_to_colours(flow)







flow


A two-channel vector field: 2 x height x width, channel 1 the row component and channel 2 the column component, which is the layout the engine’s targets use.






What it is for: debugging a separation_flows() model. A field that is right everywhere except reversed looks obviously reversed here and identical in any loss. predict() with type = “channels” is where the field comes from.
A zero vector is black, which is also what the background is, and that is honest - the background has no direction.



A height x width x 3 array of integers, 0-255.



separation_flows() for the model that predicts one.




library("rplatypus")

field <- array(0, dim = c(2, 2, 3))
field[1, 1, 1] <- 1   # pointing down
field[2, 1, 2] <- 1   # pointing right
shown <- flow_to_colours(field)
# Two directions, two hues; and no vector, no colour.
!identical(shown[1, 1, ], shown[1, 2, ]) && all(shown[2, 3, ] == 0L)

[1] TRUE
crumbs: A vector field as a picture: hue is the direction, value is the length

title: rplatypus
text:
One detector, as an entry in platypus_spec()’s models.



yolo3(
  name,
  input_shape = c(416, 416),
  channels = NULL,
  anchors = NULL,
  anchors_per_grid = NULL,
  ignore_threshold = NULL,
  score_threshold = NULL,
  nms_threshold = NULL,
  operating_point = NULL,
  min_visibility = NULL,
  box_loss = NULL,
  optimizer = NULL,
  callbacks = NULL,
  augmentation = NULL,
  epochs = NULL,
  batch_size = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  fit = NULL
)







name


Unique within a spec; names the outputs.




input_shape


c(height, width), each a multiple of 32. The three grids are the input divided by 32, 16 and 8, so a side that does not divide gives a coarsest grid that does not tile the image. Bigger is not obviously better: on BCCD, 608 bought 0.014 of mAP@0.5 for twice the training time, and the grid does not quantise a box’s centre - the strides are fixed and the offset is a continuous output, so a larger input buys more cells rather than finer ones.




channels


Channels the model takes.




anchors


Box shapes to predict offsets from, as fractions of the input size: a list of three groups, coarsest grid first, each group a list of c(width, height) pairs. COCO publishes its nine in pixels at a 416 input, so those need dividing by 416. NULL fits them to your data.




anchors_per_grid


How many anchors to fit per grid when anchors is unset. It also sets the head’s width, which is anchors_per_grid * (n_class + 5).




ignore_threshold


A cell that is not responsible for an object but whose box overlaps one this much is left unsupervised rather than trained towards "no object". Without it, a nearly-correct guess beside the responsible cell is punished, which is the one thing a detector should not learn.




score_threshold


Discard a predicted box below this confidence. Low on purpose: average precision is computed over the whole ranking, so a cut here is a ceiling on recall that no threshold chosen later can lift.




nms_threshold


Two boxes of the same class overlapping this much are one object and the lower-scoring one is dropped. Per class, so a platelet on a red cell survives.




operating_point


The confidence at which precision and recall are reported. Separate from score_threshold because they answer different questions: that one decides what is computed at all, this one decides where on the curve to stand.




min_visibility


How much of a box must survive an augmentation that removes part of the frame, as a fraction of its original area. A convention rather than a measurement; what is defensible is the direction. A box keeping two pixels of a cell teaches the model that a two-pixel fragment is a whole cell, which produces false positives everywhere, while dropping a heavily truncated object only fails to teach it about that object. Irrelevant unless a transform can lose part of the frame, which flips and rotations never do.




box_loss


How the box coordinates are scored: “offsets”, YOLOv3’s own, or “giou”. Unset uses the engine’s default, which is “offsets” - what the published bccd-yolo3 weights were trained with.
“giou” is not the better objective, and that is measured. Blood cells, three seeds each, 150 epochs, on the dataset’s own test split:



box_loss


mAP@0.5


mAP@[.50:.95]


matched IoU




giou


0.8666 ±0.0147


0.5078 ±0.0083


0.7929 ±0.0069




offsets


0.8583 ±0.0167


0.5172 ±0.0195


0.8038 ±0.0001



Average precision separates them in neither direction - both gaps are smaller than the seed spread. The overlap of the boxes it matched does separate them, and “giou” is worse by 0.011, which is 2.7 standard errors of the difference. It is also sixty times less repeatable on exactly that quantity.
The reason is visible in detection_anchors(): GIoU exists because plain IoU is a flat zero for boxes that do not touch, so it has no gradient where a detector is most wrong - and anchors fitted to blood cells already cover them at a mean IoU of 0.877, so a prediction never starts disjoint and the advantage never arrives. On data whose fitted anchors cover poorly it should be a different story, which is untested and so not claimed.
Choose it to read the loss, not to raise the score. The offsets term cannot reach zero - cross-entropy against a soft target bottoms out at that target’s entropy - so a converged run and a stalled one print the same number, near 5.9. Under “giou” the coordinate term in training_history() reads about 0.05 on training against 0.47 on validation: a localisation gap you can see, because zero means the boxes are right.




optimizer, callbacks, augmentation, epochs, batch_size


As for u_net(). There is no loss and no metrics: YOLOv3’s objective is part of its architecture, and mean average precision is not one option among several. A field that accepts a value and ignores it is worse than no field.




weights


A registry name such as “bccd-yolo3”, an hf://owner/repo/file@commit reference, or a path to a local file. The anchors come with it.




fit


Set FALSE to load weights and skip training, which is how you get boxes on an image without a GPU and an afternoon.






Anchors. Unset, they are fitted to your training boxes with k-means under an IoU distance, which is what you want: COCO’s nine anchors borrowed for blood cells cover their boxes at a mean overlap of 0.65 against 0.88 for anchors fitted to them. Fitted anchors are recorded with the run and in the sidecar when weights are exported, because a detector cannot be reloaded without them - the same weights read with other anchors decode every box scaled by a fixed factor, with plausible boxes, plausible scores, wrong places, and nothing in the output to say so.
For the same reason, naming weights and anchors together is an error: loading takes the anchors recorded beside the file, which would leave the ones here describing nothing.



One model specification.



detection_data(), plot_boxes(), available_weights()




library("rplatypus")

yolo3("cells", input_shape = c(416, 416))

$name
[1] "cells"

$architecture
[1] "yolo3"

$input_shape
[1] 416 416

attr(,"class")
[1] "platypus_detection_model" "list"                    
attr(,"task")
[1] "object_detection"

yolo3("cells", input_shape = c(416, 416), weights = "bccd-yolo3", fit = FALSE)

$name
[1] "cells"

$architecture
[1] "yolo3"

$input_shape
[1] 416 416

$weights
[1] "bccd-yolo3"

$fit
[1] FALSE

attr(,"class")
[1] "platypus_detection_model" "list"                    
attr(,"task")
[1] "object_detection"

title: rplatypus
text:
Every value plot_masks(), plot_boxes(), overlay_mask() and overlay_agreement() use when you do not give them one: which colours mean found, missed and invented, one colour per class for plot_anchors(), how much of the image an overlay lets through, how a box is labelled, and which boxes are worth drawing at all.



drawing_style()




They belong to the engine - pyplatypus.style - and are mirrored here so that drawing needs no Python. A test holds the two together, so the same call draws the same picture from either package.

text:
Detection only. On a segmentation fit this refuses by name and points at evaluate_cases(). The name carries no detection_ prefix on purpose: this is an S3 generic, so a future task gains a method under the same name rather than a second spelling of one idea.



evaluate_images(object, ...)

## S3 method for class 'platypus_fit'
evaluate_images(
  object,
  model = NULL,
  split = "validation",
  score_threshold = NULL,
  ...
)







object


A platypus_fit() on a detection specification.




…


Unused.




model


Which model, by the name in the specification. Defaults to the first.




split


Which data to score on.




score_threshold


The confidence at which the counts are read. Unset, the specification’s operating_point is used, which is what it is for: "how many were missed" is undefined over the whole ranking, where every box the model dimly considered counts as a prediction.






evaluate() gives one row per model and evaluate_classes() one row per class. This gives one row per image, which is the question asked next: not how well on average, but which pictures it fails on. A mean over a split says 0.86; it does not say the misses are four frames where the stain is dark, and that difference is usually something about the data rather than the model.
Sort by missed for the frames it cannot see, and by mean_matched_iou for the ones where it finds everything and places it badly. Those are different problems - the first is usually the data, the second usually the anchors.
There is no average precision here, deliberately. Average precision is the area under a precision-recall curve, so it is a property of a ranking over a whole dataset; computed on one image with three boxes it moves on a single box’s rank and means nothing. What is meaningful for one picture is counting and overlap, which is what the columns carry.
mean_matched_iou is NA rather than 0 when nothing matched. An image where the model found nothing and one where it found badly-placed boxes are different failures, and a zero would merge them.



A data frame of class platypus_images, one row per image: key, n_truth, n_predicted, matched, missed, spurious and mean_matched_iou.



evaluate_classes() for one row per class, evaluate_cases() for the segmentation counterpart.




library("rplatypus")

images <- evaluate_images(fit)
head(images[order(-images$missed), ])          # the frames it cannot see
head(images[order(images$mean_matched_iou), ]) # the ones it places badly

title: rplatypus
text:
One per model, and it decides the head’s width and which losses are admissible - both derived by the engine rather than stated here, so there is no channel count to get wrong. Pass the result as a model’s separation; see u_net().



separation_rim(width = NULL)

separation_flows(mode = NULL, loss = NULL, weight = NULL)







width


For rim, how many pixels wide the rim is, in the model’s input resolution. Unset uses the engine’s default, which is 2 and stands on an argument rather than on a measurement: the published sweep peaked at 3 pixels of source resolution, which on a 520-pixel case read at 256 is about 1.5 pixels of model input, and a sweep in model pixels has not been run.




mode


For flows, “diffusion” or “centroid”. Unset uses the engine’s default of “diffusion”, which stands on a measurement: decoded against the truth it reaches 0.9924 where “centroid” reaches 0.9478, because a straight line to a centroid leaves a crescent-shaped object.




loss


For flows, the objective for the vector channels, which has to be one defined over numbers rather than over classes. Unset uses the engine’s default.




weight


For flows, how much of the total objective the vector half provides.






separation_rim() trains three classes - background, object interior, object rim - and the rim is what separates two touching objects. separation_flows() trains a vector field pointing at each object’s own sink, so every foreground pixel carries a value and none of them is spent on being a boundary.
What this is worth was measured and it is not flattering. On the Data Science Bowl’s held-out cases the flow route is worth +0.0680 of instance average precision over decode_connected_components(), which ignores the signal entirely, and the rim route +0.0640 - while substituting a perfect mask is worth +0.2398. So the mask is the limit by a factor of 3.6, and a run that beats the published weights’ 0.4888 without reaching 0.7655 has improved its mask and said nothing about separation.
There is no hv. Its markers lose to a one-pixel erosion on perfect inputs, 0.9382 against 0.9807, so naming it would promise a mechanism that was measured as absent.



A separation block, to be passed as a model’s separation.



decodings, instance_data()




library("rplatypus")

separation_rim(width = 2)

$name
[1] "rim"

$width
[1] 2

separation_flows(mode = "diffusion")

$name
[1] "flows"

$mode
[1] "diffusion"

title: rplatypus
text:
One row per directory, saying whether it is a usable series and what is wrong with it if it is not. Problems are reported as a column rather than raised, because a hundred cases out of an archive will contain a few with a missing slice, two series in one folder, or duplicated files - and stopping at the first turns an afternoon’s work into a week’s.



series_report(paths)







paths


Directories, each holding the slices of one series.






Reads no pixels. Every check runs on the DICOM headers, so this is usable on a hundred gigabytes of data and is the first thing worth running on a new dataset.



A data frame with one row per directory: path, ok, slices, sorted_by, spacing_1/2/3, series_uid and problem.



A missing slice, which does not make a volume shorter - it puts everything past the gap in the wrong place, and no metric would show it. Two series in one folder, which is the normal state of an archive export: a scout, a reconstruction and a phase sitting together, which stacked would interleave two anatomies. Duplicated slices, from a copy or from several echoes mixed together. Slices of different size, angle or spacing.
It also reports how the slices were ordered. “position” means the geometry decided, which is what you want. “instance_number” means the files carry no positions and the order came from a number that is only required to be unique - worth knowing before trusting the result.



volume_info() for NIfTI files, split_dataset() for dividing the cases up.




library("rplatypus")

cases <- list.dirs("dicom_export", recursive = FALSE)
report <- series_report(cases)

report[!report$ok, c("path", "problem")]     # the ones to deal with first
table(report$sorted_by)
crumbs: Check folders of DICOM slices before training on them

title: rplatypus
text:
evaluate() gives one row per model: one number for a whole set. This gives one row per case - each image, or each patient when group_by is set - because one number hides the distribution, and the distribution is usually the finding. A model averaging Dice 0.86 that scores 0.1 on three patients has a failure mode, and the mean is where it hides.



evaluate_cases(object, ...)

## S3 method for class 'platypus_fit'
evaluate_cases(
  object,
  model = NULL,
  split = "validation",
  group_by = NULL,
  ...
)

## S3 method for class 'platypus_cases'
summary(object, ...)







object


A platypus_cases from evaluate_cases().




…


Unused.




model


Which model, by the name in the specification. Defaults to the first.




split


Which data to score on.




group_by


A pattern picking a group out of each case’s name, as in split_dataset(). With it, the rows are patients rather than slices: a patient’s slices are pooled into one score, the way a volume would be.






summary() on the result gives the distribution: mean, standard deviation, median, range, and which case scored worst.
Tiled models are scored on the whole image, not on tiles. Overlaps are accumulated across a case’s tiles and the metric applied once, which is that image’s score exactly; averaging the tiles’ scores would be a different number, and unkind to any case whose object happens to straddle a boundary.



A data frame with one row per case, of class platypus_cases.



split_dataset() for keeping a patient out of two sets in the first place.




library("rplatypus")

cases <- evaluate_cases(fit)
summary(cases)
head(cases[order(cases$dice), ])          # the ones worth looking at

evaluate_cases(fit, group_by = "^(patient\\\\d+)_")

title: rplatypus
text:
What gets reported. Unlike the losses these are computed on the hard prediction - the mask you will actually be handed - because a metric taken on probabilities reads higher than the model deserves.



metric_iou(smooth = 1, include_background = TRUE)

metric_dice(smooth = 1, include_background = TRUE)

metric_tversky(alpha = 0.5, smooth = 1, include_background = TRUE)

metric_cldice(iterations = 5, smooth = 1, include_background = FALSE)

metric_surface_dice(tau, smooth = 1, include_background = FALSE)







smooth


Smoothing. Zero is allowed and is the honest choice for a reported number: with smoothing, a class absent from an image scores a perfect 1.




include_background


Average over the background class as well. In medical images the background is usually most of the picture, so leaving it in can turn a model that found nothing into one that looks respectable. Papers report foreground only. It defaults to TRUE for the three overlap metrics and FALSE for metric_cldice() and metric_surface_dice(), where the background class does not merely flatter a model but measures something that is not the question - its skeleton and its boundary are both artefacts of the frame rather than of what was found. The paragraphs above give both measurements.




alpha


For Tversky, the weight on false negatives.




iterations


For clDice, how many times the skeleton is peeled. It has to reach the half-width of the thickest structure, or its core is never reduced to a centreline and the score is refused rather than reported - an empty skeleton otherwise reads as a perfect 1.




tau


For metric_surface_dice(), the tolerance a boundary is allowed to be wrong by, and it is required because no default would be honest. A tolerance belongs to the structure and the dataset rather than to a package: conventionally it is the inter-observer variability for that structure - the distance two people drawing the same boundary differ by - and published values exist per organ and per challenge. Take one from the protocol you are comparing against. In millimetres where target_spacing puts every case on a common grid, and in voxels where it does not, which is the same pair of answers the signed distance map in loss_boundary() gives and for the same reason: a 0.5 mm and a 2.5 mm acquisition are not comparable in voxels at all.






Three of these ask the same question and two ask different ones. metric_iou(), metric_dice() and metric_tversky() all ask how much of the mask coincides and differ in how they weigh the ways of being wrong. metric_cldice() asks whether the structure coincides, and metric_surface_dice() asks how far wrong the boundary is - which is the question a contour somebody has to approve is actually judged by, and the one nothing here reported until the pin moved to 0.8.0a26.
For something thin and connected clDice is the question worth asking, and it and Dice disagree in a way worth knowing. Measured on a nine-pixel vessel: one drawn two pixels thin scores Dice 0.875, and the same vessel severed in the middle scores 0.947 - Dice prefers the severed one. clDice gives them 1.000 and 0.943.
Its limit, also measured: at one pixel wide a displacement of one pixel leaves no overlap at all, and every overlap-based metric reads 0, this one included.
metric_surface_dice() is the other kind of disagreement. loss_boundary()’s own page reports a model at Dice 0.9525 whose volumes run 5% small and 17% wrong per case, and no overlap column says that: a displaced boundary and a correct one of the same area score alike. This is normalised surface Dice (Nikolov et al., 2018), symmetric on purpose - the truth’s surface near the prediction is the boundary’s recall, the prediction’s surface near the truth is its precision - and it is the one metric here that reads the voxel spacing, so tau is in millimetres when target_spacing has put the data on a common grid and in voxels when it has not. It is also what loss_boundary() optimises, so until now that loss was being judged by the metric it exists to improve on.
Like clDice it is a property of a whole mask rather than of a batch of counts, so on a tiled run (splits) it is reported per case by evaluate_cases() and is absent from the epoch history - a per-batch average of per-tile boundaries would be a number about nothing. A callback asking to watch val_surface_dice on such a run is refused when the configuration is read, the way one watching val_cldice is - so the choice to tile and the choice of what to stop on are settled together, before anything is trained.
include_background defaults to FALSE for those two and TRUE for the three overlap metrics, and each has its own measured reason. The background’s skeleton lies inside the background by construction, so that class scores 1 for clDice whatever the model did - averaging it in moved 0.7865 to 0.8933 on a three-pixel vessel. The background’s boundary is the foreground’s boundary plus the edge of the picture, and that edge agrees between any two masks whatever happened in them: measured on four random pairs at tau = 2, the background scored 0.6110 to 0.7030 against the foreground’s 0.5583 to 0.6266 - higher every time. That is agreement on the field of view rather than on the object.



A metric specification.




library("rplatypus")

metric_dice(include_background = FALSE)

$name
[1] "dice"

$smooth
[1] 1

$include_background
[1] FALSE

# Vessels, airways, neurons, cracks: thin and connected, where Dice asks the wrong thing.
metric_cldice()

$name
[1] "cldice"

$iterations
[1] 5

$smooth
[1] 1

$include_background
[1] FALSE

# How far wrong the boundary is, rather than how much of the area coincides. 1.5 mm
# because that is this structure's inter-observer variability, not because of anything
# here.
metric_surface_dice(tau = 1.5)

$name
[1] "surface_dice"

$tau
[1] 1.5

$smooth
[1] 1

$include_background
[1] FALSE

A callback asking to watch val_surface_dice on such a run is refused when the configuration is read, the way one watching val_cldice is - so the choice to tile and the choice of what to stop on are settled together, before anything is trained.
include_background defaults to FALSE for those two and TRUE for the three overlap metrics, and each has its own measured reason. The background’s skeleton lies inside the background by construction, so that class scores 1 for clDice whatever the model did - averaging it in moved 0.7865 to 0.8933 on a three-pixel vessel. The background’s boundary is the foreground’s boundary plus the edge of the picture, and that edge agrees between any two masks whatever happened in them: measured on four random pairs at tau = 2, the background scored 0.6110 to 0.7030 against the foreground’s 0.5583 to 0.6266 - higher every time. That is agreement on the field of view rather than on the object.



A metric specification.




library("rplatypus")

metric_dice(include_background = FALSE)

$name
[1] "dice"

$smooth
[1] 1

$include_background
[1] FALSE

# Vessels, airways, neurons, cracks: thin and connected, where Dice asks the wrong thing.
metric_cldice()

$name
[1] "cldice"

$iterations
[1] 5

$smooth
[1] 1

$include_background
[1] FALSE

# How far wrong the boundary is, rather than how much of the area coincides. 1.5 mm
# because that is this structure's inter-observer variability, not because of anything
# here.
metric_surface_dice(tau = 1.5)

$name
[1] "surface_dice"

$tau
[1] 1.5

$smooth
[1] 1

$include_background
[1] FALSE
