That is a stronger pair than the palette or the pixels: a reader who meets this warning in R and then in Python has to be told the same thing, and the pin is what makes comparing prose safe - one exact engine, so a rewording on either side fails here instead of drifting. Measured: of five mutations, changing one phrase of the message is caught by that test and by nothing else.








predict() returns the objects. It refused an instance fit until now, and the refusal was right for as long as the bridge had no call that returned a label map. A named list of integer maps, one per image, objects numbered from 1 and 0 for background.
Named rather than ordered, and that is the part worth stating: the engine’s own list is unnamed, and anything pairing two sequences by position is one dropped batch away from naming the wrong picture - the mistake predict_stream() exists on the semantic side to avoid. The names are read from the same two objects the engine pairs internally, and a test asserts they are the keys evaluate_cases() reports.
A list rather than an array for the reason the detection one is a list: images differ in size and so does the number of objects.
decode = picks which decoding turns the channels into objects, by the name in the model’s decode list. Unset takes the model’s first, which is the engine’s default rather than one restated here - and an unknown name is refused by the engine, naming the ones the model does ask for. Refused outright on a fit that decodes nothing.
instance_sizes() is one row per object: voxels, and with spacing either area_mm2 or volume_ml. The question [#103](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/103) opens with is how many nuclei, and how big is each one, which the published weights’ card cannot answer.
The unit is in the column’s name rather than in the documentation, because a column whose unit lives elsewhere ends up in a paper as a bare number. Without spacing there is no such column at all, rather than a count pretending to be a measurement. Millilitres for a volume, as [mask_volume()] reports them, and a test holds the two to the same arithmetic.
flow_to_colours() draws a two-channel vector field: hue is the direction, value is the length. A convention rather than a decision - which is why it is not in drawing_style() - and it is what makes a separation_flows() model debuggable, because a field that is right everywhere except reversed looks obviously reversed here and identical in any loss.
Pixel-identical to the engine’s on random fields, which is the only thing that can hold a convention.





type = "probability" is refused on an instance fit, by name. An instance model’s channels are not all probabilities: the class channels are and a flow field’s components are raw, because a softmax across a flow component and a class returns a number that means nothing. The engine refuses to conflate the two and so does this - the value is type = "channels", which says what it gives.
space is refused on an instance fit, with the reason rather than “unsupported”. Resampling a label map interpolates between object numbers, so object 3 beside object 5 comes back with a rim of object 4. A refusal saying only that it is not supported would read as a gap somebody might fill.





A one-row flow field had no dimensions. field[1, , ] on a 2 x 1 x w array drops to a vector, so the picture came back with no dim at all - and a tiled model hands back exactly that shape at the edge of an image. Found because the comparison against the engine ran three shapes rather than one; with only the first it would have shipped.








overlay_instances() draws an instance label map over its image, with one colour per object chosen so that no two touching objects share one. The rule is adjacency rather than identity: a colour repeats across the picture and never between neighbours, because nobody reads object 214 by its colour and everybody needs to see where one object ends.
That is an exact graph colouring - Welsh-Powell, greedy in order of descending degree - and it is affordable rather than clever. Measured in the engine over all 670 Data Science Bowl cases, 524 of which hold touching objects: the hardest needs three of the eight slots in class_colours, while the cheap alternative of colouring by object number modulo the palette paints 550 of 5436 adjacent pairs in one colour, 10.12% - one touching pair in ten drawn as a single object, in a figure whose whole subject is whether two objects are two.
Eight-connected, so two objects meeting at a corner get different colours. A label-maker goes the other way and joins only along edges, because there the risk is merging two objects into one; here the risk is drawing two as one, which is the opposite direction.
overlay_instance_agreement() is found, missed and invented objects. overlay_agreement() answers the same three-way question about pixels, and on an instance result that is the wrong unit: a merged pair and a split object are both nearly perfect pixelwise and both wrong, which is what an average precision will not tell anybody. Matched whole object against whole object at one IoU threshold, strictly greater, and below 0.5 is refused for the reason the metric refuses it.





The matching needs no greedy pass, and that is provable rather than convenient. The engine matches greedily on descending IoU; this package matches every pair above the threshold, which is equivalent above 0.5: if two disjoint true objects both exceeded 0.5 against one prediction, each intersection would exceed half of it - the union is at least the prediction - and two disjoint intersections cannot together exceed it. So the matching is one to one whatever order it is taken in, which is also why the metric refuses a lower threshold.
Written as the equivalent rather than as a copy because argsort is not stable: two pairs at the same IoU leave the engine in an order neither package controls, and a pixel-for-pixel test would then fail for something that is not a divergence.





Nothing held the two packages to the same colouring, and the shared constant could not. [#154](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/154)’s subject: the palette is mirrored and test-drawing-style.R holds it, so the two would keep agreeing about which eight colours while disagreeing about which object gets which. tests/testthat/test-instance-drawing.R draws the same pictures both ways and compares them pixel for pixel - five label maps including three objects each touching the other two, and five ways an instance result goes wrong - which is the only thing that can hold a rule rather than a constant.
Six mutations, each caught: four-connected instead of eight, colour by object number instead of by adjacency, ascending instead of descending degree, >= instead of > at the threshold, and two ways of getting the outline wrong. The outline pair needed a new picture: against the first one both mutations passed, because every object in it was three pixels across and had no interior to lose. §4’s “a check calibrated loosely enough admits the failure it was written to prevent”, found by mutating rather than by reading.
flow_to_colours() is still deferred, and the stated reason has expired. [#154](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/154) defers it because “R cannot configure flows until pyplatypus[#160](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/160)” - which shipped in 0.8.0a20, and separation_flows() has been exported here since. The reason that holds now is a different one: predict() refuses an instance fit, so there is no way to get a flow field into R to draw. It belongs with [#103](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/103), where the prediction comes back.








segmentation_data(regions = ), the third way of saying what a mask’s classes are and the only one that lets a voxel belong to more than one. A list of list(name = , of = ), where of holds the label-map values making up that region:
segmentation_data(
  "train/", "valid/",
  regions = list(list(name = "whole tumour", of = c(1, 2, 4)),
                 list(name = "enhancing", of = 4))
)
That is the BraTS shape, and the second entry shows that a single value is ordinary rather than an edge case. The engine has had the field since 0.8.0a14; R forwarding it was a code change rather than a pin bump, which is worth saying because the first guess was the opposite: segmentation_data() enumerates its parameters, so regions was an unused argument while a bare data list and a YAML file both reached the engine’s own validator and were accepted. The constructor refusing what YAML took is the asymmetry this closes. pyplatypus[#91](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/91), [#152](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/152).
Two things ?segmentation_data now says that the field name does not. There is no background entry, so n_class is not the number it would be for that many labels. And each channel is an independent binary question - a sigmoid per channel rather than one softmax across them - so a voxel may be in several regions at once, which is the point.
The configuration vignette has a section on overlapping classes, Overlapping classes instead of one per voxel, between the augmentation section and the instance one - because regions is still semantic_segmentation and what changes is what a channel means rather than what the task is. The section list is pinned by a test here and by the same list in the engine’s suite, so it landed in both repositories together: pyplatypus[#229](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/229) first, because this side compares itself against that list.
Two things in it are R’s own: a region is a list(name = , of = ) and the last one shows that of = 4 is ordinary rather than an edge case, and inspect_masks() names the region that matched nothing instead of giving its position. Both the YAML block and the R chunk are validated - checked by breaking each, which fails the test that reads it rather than passing quietly.
inspect_masks() names regions rather than numbering them. The engine reports classes by position, and with regions a position is the one thing a reader cannot resolve: missing_classes: 1 means the second region, and counting entries in a configuration file to find out which is the step nobody takes. With colormap or labels the number is the class, so it stays a number - naming it would invent something the specification did not say, and a test holds that.
It matters most for the one failure regions invites: of = 3 against a label map holding 4 is a channel of zeros, so the model trains to predict nothing and scores a Dice of 0 for that region while every other number in the run looks ordinary.
The positions are still attached as the present and missing attributes, so anything reading them keeps working. The mapping is derived in R from the specification R owns rather than asked of the engine - which would mean a release and a pin move for a label - and what holds the two together is a test comparing R’s name against the engine’s own refusal sentence. An off-by-one in that mapping fails it, which is the one mistake whose output otherwise looks entirely ordinary.
The exclusivity check is three-way and names what was given. One of colormap, labels and regions, in one message, matching the engine’s own sentence - and the message now says which arguments it found rather than only that one was expected.
save_class_masks() writes an overlapping prediction, one file per class. Needs pyplatypus 0.8.0a23, which is what the pin moves to here, and where the writer lives; this side forwards to it rather than keeping a second copy of the rules, because the filenames are part of what somebody’s next script reads. <name><suffix>_<class>.png, black and white, and a class name becomes a filename by replacing anything a path cannot hold with _ - so whole tumour is whole_tumour. Two class names that become the same filename are refused rather than written: one file would hold the second class, the first would be silently gone, and the number of returned paths would still be right.
The argument is classes and not names, which is §3A applied before the surface existed: names in this family is the files - save_masks() and save_volumes() both use it that way - and a sibling writer where the same word means the classes instead would accept a call copied from one to the other whenever the counts happened to match. The engine’s own function calls them classes too, for the same reason.





save_masks() and save_volumes() refuse an overlapping prediction instead of silently reducing it. Both took which.max over the channel axis, which for sigmoid channels writes one of the classes a voxel is in and leaves nothing in the file to say so. They now count how many channels are hot at the most ambitious voxel and refuse with that number, each pointing at its own per-class writer.
[#152](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/152) named save_masks() and there turned out to be three reduction sites, not one: save_volumes() has two, a 4-dimensional array inside a list and a 5-dimensional stack. Found by asking what a BraTS user would actually run, which is §4’s a feature is not shipped until something has used it the way a user reaches it applied to a refusal.
Detected from the array rather than from the specification, which is the same test the engine applies in onehot_to_colours - so both halves refuse the same arrays, and a caller holding only a prediction can answer the question. A softmax prediction never trips it, since its channels sum to one and at most one can reach half; that control is a test rather than a sentence, because without it every ordinary run would start refusing.
save_class_volumes() is the same thing for volumes, and it is the case regions was built for. BraTS names three overlapping regions and stores them as volumes, so a writer that only handled pictures would have left the motivating dataset with a refusal and no route to disk. One NIfTI per class, each carrying the geometry of the scan it was predicted from - which is the whole reason this is not save_class_masks() with another extension.
It needs no engine release: it goes through the same volume writer save_volumes() uses, so the affine, the integer labels and the grid check are those rather than a second copy. What is a second copy is the rule turning a class name into a filename, because the volume path never reaches the engine’s class_filename - so a test holds R’s rule to the engine’s over the names that are actually awkward, rather than a comment claiming they agree.
predict(type = "class") refused rather than computed when the classes overlap, and "class" is the default, so this is the first call an R user makes on such a fit. There is no one class per pixel to return: the channels are independent binary questions, they do not compete, and an argmax across them names one of the classes a pixel is in. The refusal says to ask for type = "probability" and names what writes it.
Read off the specification the fit carries, which is a lever this package owns - the shape cannot answer it, because sigmoid channels and a softmax’s channels are the same array.
A single of value would have crossed over as a number rather than a list. reticulate turns a length-1 integer vector into a Python scalar, and the schema wants an array, so of = 4 had to be built with as.list(). Measured both ways before the code was written, and the engine refuses the scalar - so this would have been a refusal nobody could read rather than a silent wrong answer, on the most ordinary region there is.
Still in [#152](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/152), deliberately not here, and written as a paragraph rather than a heading because R CMD check reads every ### in this file as a version and says so: save_masks() refusing an overlapping prediction and the per-class writer that replaces it, inspect_masks() naming regions rather than numbering them, and the guide section. Each is independently worth having, which is why none waits for the others.

title: Change Log
text:
A different package from 0.1.1 under the same name, and the section below says how different.


This was in the README until 2026-10-07 - seventy lines between ## Installing and the first example, about a version the reader does not have, before the one they do. It is here because this file is where R keeps what changed between versions, and because the renames table below was a second copy of one the README already carried; the fuller of the two survived.
Code written against the 2020 release will not run on this one. That version built Keras models through the R keras package and handed them back to you; this one describes a whole run as a specification and computes it in PyTorch. Of the 37 functions and objects the old version exported, 30 are gone — including all of yolo3(), darknet53(), load_darknet_weights(), get_boxes(), non_max_suppression(), plot_boxes(), segmentation_generator() and the annotation readers.
Seven names survive, and three of them are the ones to watch, because they are still exported, still callable, and mean something different:








name
0.1.1
now




u_net()
u_net(net_h, net_w, grayscale, ...) → a Keras model
u_net(name, input_shape, ...) → one model in a specification


plot_masks()
plot_masks(images_paths, masks, labels, colormap)
plot_masks(images, prediction, truth, ...)


loss_dice()
no arguments, returns a Keras loss
loss_dice(smooth = 1), returns a loss to name in a specification



The other four — binary_colormap, voc_colormap, binary_labels, voc_labels — are the same data as before.
Object detection is back, and the names are different. The old package handed you a Keras YOLOv3; this one describes a detector in a specification like everything else. So those five names are gone rather than moved, and what replaces them is:







0.1.1
now




yolo3(), darknet53()
yolo3() as one entry in platypus_spec() - same name, a specification rather than a model


load_darknet_weights()
weights = "bccd-yolo3", or a path, or hf://owner/repo/file@commit


get_boxes(), non_max_suppression()
done inside predict(), which returns boxes already suppressed and in each image’s own pixels


plot_boxes()
plot_boxes() - same name, takes what predict() returns



The annotation readers are gone as functions and are now what detection_data() reads for you: Pascal VOC XML or LabelMe JSON, named rather than guessed.
The old release is still there and still installable, pinned:
remotes::install_github("maju116/rplatypus@0.1.1")
Its source is on the master branch, and the issues filed against it stay open. What has aged is its dependencies rather than its code: the pinned TensorFlow no longer installs on a current Python, which is the reason for a rewrite rather than a consequence of one.






library(platypus) is library(rplatypus). The name collided with Platypus, archived from CRAN on 2026-02-02 - unrelated work in immunology - and the two differed only in case, which the policy treats as a conflict and which archiving does not release. cran-comments.md had promised to resubmit under another name rather than ask for an exception, so this is that name rather than a new idea: one name per language, beside the pyplatypus engine on PyPI, and a name that says what the package is - the R surface over a Python engine.
rplatypus is in neither CRAN’s current index nor its archive, checked against both with a positive control so that the absence means something.
The functions did not change. platypus_spec(), platypus_fit(), platypus_status(), platypus_device() and platypus_use_torch() keep their names, and so do the S3 classes platypus_fit, platypus_spec, platypus_split and the rest, the platypus_* condition classes, the PLATYPUS_* environment variables and the headers print() writes. The rule is that the package’s identity - what library() and CRAN see - is rplatypus, and the brand is still platypus. §3A already said the S3 class keeps the prefix even where its constructor loses it; this is the same line drawn one level up, and it means no released surface moved.
The repository was renamed too, to maju116/rplatypus. Stars, forks, watchers and every issue came with it - read back from the API rather than assumed - and github.com/maju116/platypus redirects, so links in other people’s issue comments keep working. The site moved with the repository and is now at maju116.github.io/rplatypus; the former address has no redirect, because a project page is served under the repository’s own name and the only way to hold the old one would be to occupy the name the redirect needs.
The dated entries below name maju116/platypus where they were written that way. They are the record of what it was called at the time and they still resolve, so they are left alone rather than rewritten.





This file has a gap and it is named rather than backfilled. The entry below is dated 2026-10-08 and the pin moved twice between then and here - to 0.8.0a12 for fives-unet ([#151](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/151)) and to 0.8.0a20 for the instance task ([#155](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/155)) - so the dates above this heading are not a complete record of what the pin did. Writing those entries now would be writing them from the commit log rather than from the work, which is a different thing from having written them; the heading says what this change is and the omission stays visible.



Engine pinned to 0.8.0a22, for two things R forwards rather than implements.
A regression loss is refused as any segmentation model’s own loss, not only an instance model’s. ?losses claimed the narrower rule and was measured when it was written, so it was true rather than wrong - the engine’s refusal lived on the instance class alone, and a semantic model accepted loss_mse() and trained with it, reporting a validation loss of 0.0014 for a mask that was half missing where loss_cce() reaches a Dice of 1.0000. The default where = "foreground" is what made that look like a success: it averages the objective only inside the labelled objects and leaves the background unconstrained. pyplatypus[#223](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/223).
So available_losses() is ten rows now rather than thirteen, and available_losses("instance_segmentation") is thirteen - the three regression losses are reachable where they have a target, which is separation_flows(loss = ). Nothing R sends changes: a configuration refused after this pin move was refused by the engine before it.
evaluate() on an instance fit carries foreground_dice. It is the mask column to read across models - the binary overlap of anything the model called an object against anything that is one, the same arithmetic whatever the separation is. The dice beside it is a mean over the class channels the head has, three for separation_rim() against two for separation_flows(), so it is read down one model’s rows and never across two: on the Data Science Bowl’s validation cases it showed two masks 0.09 apart that are 0.0062 apart, and in the other direction. pyplatypus[#222](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/222).





?losses’ task parameter listed two tasks and there have been three since the engine’s 0.8.0a20.








metric_cldice(), for structures where Dice asks the wrong question. It scores each mask against the other’s skeleton, so it measures whether a vessel is connected rather than whether its pixels coincide. Vessels, airways, neurons, cracks, catheters.
The two disagree in a way worth knowing, measured on a nine-pixel vessel: one drawn two pixels thin scores Dice 0.875, and the same vessel severed in the middle scores 0.947 - Dice prefers the severed one. clDice gives them 1.000 and 0.943. Its limit is measured too: at one pixel wide, a one-pixel displacement leaves no overlap at all and every overlap-based metric reads 0, this one included.
include_background defaults to FALSE here and TRUE for the other three. The background’s skeleton lies inside the background by construction, so that class scores 1 whatever the model did.





Engine pinned to 0.8.0a2.








drawing_style(), the five decisions every figure in this package makes when you do not give it one: which colours mean found, missed and invented, how much of the image an overlay lets through, how a box is labelled, and which boxes are worth drawing. Reach for it when you want to match a figure rather than restate it - colours = drawing_style()$box_colours keeps one source where typing the hex codes starts a second.





The drawing decisions now come from the engine. They were written out in ten places across R/plot.R and R/masks.R, and pyplatypus.style held the same five values - which is two copies that happened to agree, not one source. They agreed because five differences between the two packages’ figures had been found by laying them side by side and fixing them by hand.
Nothing changes in any picture: the values are identical, and a test compares every one of them against the engine’s, so a change on that side now fails this package’s CI instead of being noticed by eye.
Drawing still needs no Python. That is why the values are mirrored in R/style.R rather than fetched: plot_masks(), plot_boxes() and overlay_agreement() return without touching the bridge, and a default colour that called the engine would mean a five-gigabyte download to draw a mask.








Eight functions were renamed. The engine and this package had grown two words for the same thing in eight places, and a reader moving between the halves paid for every one. One name per concept now, and where the two disagreed the engine’s name won, because it is the layer that cannot be renamed later without changing the configuration format and the schema. The exception is available_transforms(), where this package already had a family of available_* names and the engine followed instead.








was
is
why




platypus_split()
split_dataset()
the engine’s name. The S3 class is still platypus_split - that is the object’s identity, and every class here is prefixed


split_files()
split_path()
it reads one split’s path; it does not split files. split_samples() in the engine is a different function, and the two names invited pairing them


mask_report()
inspect_masks()
the engine’s name, and the method it calls


mask_classes()
colours_to_classes()
the engine’s name, and it says which way the conversion goes


mask_colours()
classes_to_colours()
likewise. Note the engine’s onehot_to_colours() is not this function - it takes probabilities and argmaxes them, this takes class indices


save_weights()
export_weights()
the engine’s name; “export” says a sidecar is written beside the file


available_augmentations()
available_transforms()
the engine’s name, and albumentations’ own word for them


augment()
augmentation_step()
augment is a generic in broom and means something else there. augmentation alone would have shadowed the augmentation = argument it builds a list for



No aliases: two names for one thing is what this removes. The S3 class returned by split_dataset() is still platypus_split - that is the object’s identity, and every class in the package is prefixed.
evaluate(), evaluate_cases(), evaluate_classes() and evaluate_images() keep their names and so does platypus_fit(). The prefix on that one is not an inconsistency: fit is a generic in the tidymodels packages, so a bare fit would have been theirs to own, while evaluate is a generic here and dispatches on the fit’s class whichever package was attached last.
PYPLATYPUS_VERSION is pyplatypus_version. It was the only ALL-CAPS name in the package, so keeping it would have meant a lint exception for a style used exactly once.





callback_swa(): average the weights over the last part of the run. What it is worth is not in the score column - Dice and per-case error do not move - it is in the spread. Measured over three seeds, the volume bias went from +4.5% / +12.2% / -11.6% to -0.1% / +4.2% / +2.1%, 5.7 times tighter. The help page says so in those words, because somebody reading “weight averaging” will look at Dice, find nothing, and conclude wrongly. Refused beside callback_cosine_annealing(): a cosine has decayed to its floor by the time averaging begins, so the average is the last epoch.
segmentation_data(validation = FALSE): say a run has no validation set. The third answer to the question a path and a split already answered, and it had to be a stated value rather than an absence, because “I have no validation set” and “I forgot” look identical and only one of them is a decision. It went in the same argument rather than a new one, so nothing can contradict it.





The Python shim shipped inside this package is now formatted and linted by ruff in CI, beside lintr. It had never been.






The site is Quarto, not pkgdown, generated from tools/reference-groups.yml into a sidebar nested in eight groups, and themed from a _brand.yml that is byte-identical to pyplatypus’s - so the two sites look alike by construction rather than by anybody remembering to copy a colour.
Every old address still works. 105 redirect stubs cover all 99 addresses the pkgdown site published, the eight renames among them.







segmentation_data(split = ) and detection_data(split = ): divide one training folder into splits without writing any files. The argument is a list of fractions (two numbers, or three to cut a test set too) and group_by, which is a required key that may be NULL. The mistake it prevents leaves no trace: slices of one patient on both sides make validation measure memory rather than generalisation, and nothing in the output says so. An omitted key would be that choice made silently; NULL is the same choice made on purpose. For detection this is the only way to divide one folder, because split_dataset() writes a masks column.
detection_crops(): cut the detected objects out of the images they were found in, at a fixed size, for handing to a classifier. Crops come from the source image through the same reader the dataset uses, are rounded outward so the whole box survives, and letterbox rather than stretch.
yolo3(box_loss = "giou"). Measured on BCCD over three seeds, 150 epochs, it is worse on the metric it targets - matched overlap 0.7929 against 0.8038, established at 2.7 standard errors - and its spread is sixty times wider. It ships because its coordinate term reads zero when the boxes are right, where the default term cannot reach zero however right they are. ?yolo3 leads with that table, because the name invites choosing it and the measured answer is the other way.
loss_boundary(): a region loss plus the signed distance to the truth’s boundary. region and alpha default to NULL here and are left out of the request, so the engine’s own defaults apply - alpha = 0.9, which it pins with a test, because at 0.5 the surface term owns half the objective while the prediction is still random and the volume bias spread goes to +/-28%. What the loss trades is accuracy per case for being unbiased over a series: measured over three seeds, the systematic volume bias went from -5.18% to -0.06% and the per-case absolute error from 16.90% to 22.17%.





Every help page has an \examples section but one - 47 of 48 at the time, encoders being a concept page with no \usage - and a test parses every example in every .Rd, including inside \dontrun{}, and fails if it names a function that does not exist. What was at risk was never the functionality; it is the example text drifting from the API.
lintr runs over the package in CI and gates on its findings. Of 906 findings at lintr’s defaults, 890 were the 80-character line limit this package does not use; at 100 characters and lint_package(), 25 - two of which were defects rather than style.






evaluate_images(): one row per image for a detector - n_truth, n_predicted, matched, missed, spurious, mean_matched_iou. Order by missed for the frames it cannot see, by mean_matched_iou for the ones where it finds everything and places it badly. No average precision per image: AP is the area under a ranking’s curve and on one picture it moves on a single box.
platypus_spec(task = ) can be stated, and is checked rather than trusted - it can confirm or refuse, never override. Unset, it is still derived from the constructors. Required in YAML and optional here is not an inconsistency: task is needed exactly where the type is not already stated, and segmentation_data() with u_net() can only mean one thing.





Object detection, from R. detection_data(), yolo3(), detection_anchors(), plot_boxes(), and predict() returning a list of boxes in each image’s own pixels - not an array, because images differ in size, so does the number of boxes, and a box in a letterboxed frame cannot be drawn on the photograph it came from.
plot_anchors(): the fitted anchors against the boxes they were fitted to. It is in the vignette twice, on the split they were fitted on and the one they were not.
A README figure for detection, drawn by the published bccd-yolo3 with no training, and tools/readme_figures.R that reproduces it.
Corrected: the claim that COCO’s anchors cover BCCD’s boxes at 0.67 where fitted ones reach 0.92. Re-measured on the 2,805 real training boxes, the honest pair is 0.65 against 0.88. The direction survives and is large; both numbers were wrong in opposite directions and the gap was right by coincidence.





u_net(encoder = "resnet34", pretrained = TRUE), with freeze_encoder and encoder_learning_rate. pretrained is a separate explicit flag so that naming a backbone never downloads anything nobody asked for. Measured on three datasets, pretraining never clearly beats the built-in encoder; what it buys is epochs, and what a swappable encoder buys is capacity where the target is thin. The help page carries the table.
inspect_masks() and platypus_fit(check_masks = FALSE): a declared class appearing in no mask has a target channel that is zero everywhere, so the model is never shown what it is being asked to find, and platypus_fit() now refuses on it. A threshold on the unmatched fraction cannot do this job - on a 0.6% lesion a wholly wrong colormap is quieter than JPEG artefacts in healthy data.
Every help page renders its markdown. DESCRIPTION had no Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE) although every page had been written in markdown since the rewrite began, so not one cross-reference was a link: 0 to 42 links, 0 to 266 inline code spans, 36 of 40 pages changed. Nothing in the sources was wrong; nothing was converting them.





predict(space = "source"): map a prediction back out of the model’s grid onto the grid of the scan it came from, undoing the resampling and the crop. Returns a list, and the type change is the API being honest - scans differ in size, and quietly resizing them to match is how a mask ends up describing anatomy it was not computed from.
Named weights. weights = "dsbowl-unet" from the registry, hf://owner/repo/file@commit, or a local path, plus export_weights() for your own. A registry name carries a commit and the hf:// form requires one, because weights that change under a stable name are the worst kind of irreproducibility.
The Data Science Bowl vignette now opens with a mask in four lines - published weights, fit = FALSE, plot_masks() - before any mention of training. First contact should not need a GPU and an afternoon.
Fixed, and found by writing that vignette: weights = "dsbowl-unet" could not work from R at all. The bridge asked for pyplatypus with no extras, so huggingface_hub was never in the environment reticulate builds. Nothing in either test suite could have caught it - the engine’s tests install the extra deliberately and the R tests ran where it was already present.
The README says what changed since 0.1.1, written by diffing the two NAMESPACE files rather than from memory: of 0.1.1’s 37 exports, 30 are gone, and three of the seven survivors are worse than gone because they are still callable and mean something else.




The day the package stopped being a bridge and became a surface. Five engine releases, each followed here.

A worked vignette on the Data Science Bowl, precomputed so that reading it needs no GPU, and a README.
Continuous integration: five R CMD check jobs - Ubuntu on R devel, release and oldrel-1, plus macOS and Windows on release - and an engine job that installs the built package and runs the suite against the engine resolved from PyPI. That last one is the job that matters: pkgload::load_all() exposes a package’s internals, library() does not, and local work had been using the most permissive of the three ways a test can reach them.
Plotting and masks: plot_masks(), plot_boxes(), overlay_mask(), overlay_agreement(), read_masks(), unite_masks(), mask_coverage().
DICOM, properly: modality LUT, a fixed window, MONOCHROME1 inverted. Plus series_report() for a folder of slices, whose decision is that a problem is a column, not an exception - a hundred cases contain a few bad ones, and stopping at the first turns an afternoon into a week.
Splitting by patient (split_dataset(), split_path()) and evaluate_cases().
Volumes. input_shape = c(64, 64, 32) had been building a 3D U-Net since the first release; what was missing was reading NIfTI, where orientation is the whole problem, and labels as a second way to describe a mask, because volumes label with integers. save_volumes() writes NIfTI carrying the affine of the scan the mask was predicted from - without it a mask cannot be laid over its scan by any viewer, and the file looks perfectly normal while being wrong. mask_volume() reports millilitres, because a voxel count is meaningless outside one scanner.
target_spacing: resample to a common voxel size. What makes it necessary is not slice thickness but field of view - forty slices of 1 mm is 40 mm of patient and forty of 2.5 mm is 100 mm, which is the ordinary state of clinical data.
channels_from: one channel per file, stating the order and never inferring it. A model trained with FLAIR in channel one and used where channel one is T1 answers plausibly, with the right shape and range, and nothing downstream can tell.
Augmentation in 3D, and available_transforms(rank = 3) to say what is usable - 97 of albumentations’ transforms accept a volume and the rest raise from inside the library.
A second vignette, on volumes, which generates its own data. It ends on a model at Dice 0.88 whose volumes are 12-23% too large, which is the argument for reporting volume beside overlap: Dice is dominated by an object’s interior and forgiving about its boundary.
segmentation_data(window = ) replaced dicom_window, since NIfTI needs the same thing. The old name is still accepted; giving both is an error.




The package exists.

The bridge. py_require() plus uv, resolving an isolated ephemeral environment at library(rplatypus) - deliberately not the shared-Python arrangement that broke this package’s Keras stack in 2020. platypus_status() says what it found rather than leaving a failed import to be guessed at, and PLATYPUS_ENGINE_PATH points the bridge at a source tree during development.
platypus_spec(), built either from arguments or from a YAML file and producing the same thing. One pipeline, two constructors.
platypus_fit(), evaluate(), predict(), training_history(), and the engine’s complaints translated into R conditions rather than passed through as Python tracebacks.

title: Change Log
text:
The last release of the TensorFlow package, kept here for the record rather than as an ancestor of the entries above. It built Keras models through the R keras package: yolo3() and darknet53() with load_darknet_weights() for the original Darknet weights, a plain u_net(), segmentation_generator(), loss_dice(), the COCO and VOC colormaps, and readers for LabelMe JSON and Pascal VOC XML.
It is still installable and still pinned:
remotes::install_github("maju116/rplatypus@0.1.1")
Its source is on the master branch and the issues filed against it stay open. What has aged is its dependencies rather than its code - the pinned TensorFlow no longer installs on a current Python, which is the reason for a rewrite rather than a consequence of one.

title: rplatypus
text:
u_net() and the other model constructors take an encoder, which replaces the built-in contracting path with a backbone architecture, and a separate pretrained flag that loads that backbone’s ImageNet weights. This page is the measurement behind them, because the honest summary is narrower than the idea.




u_net("polyps", input_shape = c(256, 256),
      encoder = "resnet34",      # the architecture
      pretrained = TRUE,         # and its ImageNet weights
      freeze_encoder = 5)        # held still while the decoder settles


Two flags rather than one, so naming an architecture never reaches the network on a machine that has none - a hospital network often has none.



Measured on three datasets, one per modality, three seeds each, every configuration compared at its best validation Dice with the best weights restored. Training sets of 40 to 100 images on purpose, because that is the regime transfer learning is for.



configuration


DS Bowl, microscopy


SIIM-ACR, chest X-ray


Kvasir-SEG, endoscopy




built-in encoder, 1.9M parameters


0.8460


0.0531


0.5830




encoder = “resnet34”, 9.0M


0.7891


0.1073


0.5670




the same, pretrained, freeze_encoder = 5


0.8333


0.1203


0.5932




the same, encoder_learning_rate = lr/10


0.8326


0.1011


0.5329



Four things come out of it, and each repeats on all three:


Use freeze_encoder, not encoder_learning_rate alone


Freezing was the better of the two everywhere. On Kvasir a tenth of the rate is the worst row in the table - below the built-in encoder and below the same backbone trained from nothing. Giving one rate to the whole network is worse still: a randomly initialised decoder’s gradients undo the transferred weights before the decoder has learned anything worth having.


Do not expect a better score


The best pretrained configuration beats the built-in encoder on one dataset of three, by 0.0102, against a seed-to-seed spread of 0.0170 - inside the noise. And endoscopy is the fairest test available within medical imaging: camera photographs of tissue, three channels, natural lighting. With the backbone frozen for a whole run on DS Bowl the score is 0.6068 against 0.8460, so the features genuinely do not transfer to these images.


Expect to reach the same score sooner


On Kvasir the built-in encoder needed 150, 110 and 83 epochs across its three seeds; pretrained and frozen needed 64, 82 and 83. That halving is the one benefit that showed up consistently, and on a dataset that takes a day to train it is the difference that matters.


A bigger encoder earns its place where the target is thin


On SIIM-ACR, where a pneumothorax covers a median 0.59% of the frame, every backbone variant roughly doubles the built-in encoder’s score - and the built-in encoder’s spread between seeds there (0.0586) is larger than its own mean, with two of three seeds never learning at all. This is a reason to be able to swap the encoder that has nothing to do with ImageNet.


Measure on your own images before trusting any of this: the regime where transfer helps is narrow, and three public datasets are three public datasets. The engine ships examples/compare_pretrained_encoders.py, which is this measurement parameterised.



Any convolutional family timm names, as timm names it: “resnet18”, “resnet34”, “resnet50”, “resnext50_32x4d”, “efficientnet_b0” through “b3”, “mobilenetv3_large_100”, “densenet121”, “regnety_040”, “vgg16”, “inception_v3” and others. blocks then says how many of the backbone’s stages to use.
Two kinds are refused rather than approximated:


A 3D input_shape. ImageNet is images, so there is nothing to transfer to a volume. Refused while the specification is read, before anything is downloaded.


The patch-based families (“convnext_”, ”swin_”). Their features begin at a quarter of the input, so the half-resolution level a U-shaped decoder recovers fine detail from does not exist. Inventing it would put a made-up level exactly where the detail comes from.


The finest level is always platypus’s own: every ImageNet stem halves the input, so no backbone has a full-resolution feature, and the decoder’s output head sits on one. That stage is trained from scratch, which is why freeze_encoder and encoder_learning_rate leave it alone - it is the one part with everything to learn.



Nothing to do. The environment this package builds always includes the backbones, which cost 10 MB against PyTorch’s own several hundred - not a trade worth making anyone opt into. On a GTX 10-series card or older see platypus_use_torch().



models for the arguments, platypus_spec() for the specification.

Pretrained encoders, and what they are worth

title: rplatypus
text:
A quick sanity check before training: a foreground of half a percent is a problem the loss has to be chosen for, and it is better to know before the run than after.



mask_coverage(mask, labels = NULL)







mask


Class indices, counted from 1.




labels


Optional names for the classes.






A data frame with one row per class.




library("rplatypus")

mask <- matrix(1L, 8, 8); mask[2:4, 2:4] <- 2L
mask_coverage(mask, labels = c("background", "nucleus"))

  class      label pixels fraction
1     1 background     55 0.859375
2     2    nucleus      9 0.140625

# A class with 0 pixels is the thing to look for: its target channel is zero
# everywhere, so there is no gradient towards it and the model is never shown
# what it is being asked to find.

title: rplatypus
text:
Weights are named rather than downloaded by hand, and a name is pinned to one commit of the repository holding it - so “dsbowl-unet” means one set of numbers today and the same set next year. This lists what is published, with the commit each name resolves to.



available_weights()




Read the descriptions rather than only the names. A model’s limitations decide whether it answers your question: the nuclei weights are semantic, so touching nuclei come back as one region and a count taken from them would be wrong.



A data frame with name, repo, filename, revision and description.



u_net() and the other architectures, whose weights argument takes a name from here, a hf://owner/repo/file.safetensors@commit reference, or a path to a local file.




library("rplatypus")

available_weights()

spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data("images/", "images/", colormap = binary_colormap),
  models = list(u_net("nuclei", input_shape = c(256, 256), blocks = 4, filters = 16,
                      weights = "dsbowl-unet", fit = FALSE))
)
masks <- predict(platypus_fit(spec), split = "validation")

title: rplatypus
text:
Divides one directory of samples into three sets and writes each as a CSV the specification can point at. Nothing is copied: the files stay where they are and the CSVs list them, which matters when the data is large or read-only.



split_dataset(
  root,
  out_dir,
  group_by = NULL,
  fractions = c(0.7, 0.15, 0.15),
  seed = 0,
  mode = c("nested_dirs", "config_file"),
  subdirs = c("images", "masks"),
  column_sep = ";",
  strict = TRUE,
  relative = TRUE
)







root


The directory holding the samples, laid out as mode describes.




out_dir


Where to write train.csv, validation.csv and test.csv.




group_by


A pattern picking the group out of a sample’s name; see above. NULL treats every sample as its own group, which is right when one sample is one patient.




fractions


Two or three shares that add up to 1: train, validation and optionally test. Measured in samples, not in groups, so patients with very different numbers of slices do not skew them.




seed


Makes the split reproducible. The same inputs and seed give the same split on any machine and in any file order - without that, two runs are not comparable and the reason for a difference is impossible to find.




mode


“nested_dirs” for one directory per sample, “config_file” for a CSV.




subdirs


The image and mask subdirectory names, for nested_dirs.




column_sep


Separator between several paths in one CSV cell.




strict


Treat an incomplete sample as an error rather than skipping it.




relative


Write paths relative to the CSV where possible, so the dataset and its split can be moved together.






A platypus_split: the three paths, plus how many samples and groups each set received. Pass it straight to segmentation_data().



Splitting per file is the obvious thing and, for medical images, the wrong one. A scan is many slices of one patient, so dividing slices at random puts the same anatomy in training and in validation at once. The model then meets the neighbouring slice of what it is being tested on, validation measures memory rather than generalisation, and Dice comes out several points too high with nothing in the result to say so.
group_by names the unit that must not be split - usually a patient, sometimes a study, a scanner or a site. Every sample sharing a group lands in exactly one set.



group_by is passed to the engine exactly as written, and read there as a Python regular expression. In practice the dialects agree on everything you are likely to need


^, $, \d, [A-Z], +, *, () - and R’s own quoting rules still apply, so a backslash is doubled: “^(patient\\d+)_“. It is not translated on the way through, deliberately: a translation that quietly got it wrong would produce a working split with the wrong groups in it, which is the failure this argument exists to prevent.


A pattern that matches no sample is an error, never a fallback to one-group-per-sample.



evaluate_cases(), which reports a score per case rather than one per set.




library("rplatypus")

split <- split_dataset(
  "scans", "splits",
  group_by = "^(patient\\\\d+)_",
  fractions = c(0.7, 0.15, 0.15)
)
split

spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data(split, colormap = binary_colormap),
  models = list(u_net("unet", input_shape = c(256, 256)))
)

title: rplatypus
text:
Divides one directory of samples into three sets and writes each as a CSV the specification can point at. Nothing is copied: the files stay where they are and the CSVs list them, which matters when the data is large or read-only.



split_dataset(
  root,
  out_dir,
  group_by = NULL,
  fractions = c(0.7, 0.15, 0.15),
  seed = 0,
  mode = c("nested_dirs", "config_file"),
  subdirs = c("images", "masks"),
  column_sep = ";",
  strict = TRUE,
  relative = TRUE
)







root


The directory holding the samples, laid out as mode describes.




out_dir


Where to write train.csv, validation.csv and test.csv.




group_by


A pattern picking the group out of a sample’s name; see above. NULL treats every sample as its own group, which is right when one sample is one patient.




fractions


Two or three shares that add up to 1: train, validation and optionally test. Measured in samples, not in groups, so patients with very different numbers of slices do not skew them.




seed


Makes the split reproducible. The same inputs and seed give the same split on any machine and in any file order - without that, two runs are not comparable and the reason for a difference is impossible to find.




mode


“nested_dirs” for one directory per sample, “config_file” for a CSV.




subdirs


The image and mask subdirectory names, for nested_dirs.




column_sep


Separator between several paths in one CSV cell.




strict


Treat an incomplete sample as an error rather than skipping it.




relative


Write paths relative to the CSV where possible, so the dataset and its split can be moved together.

title: rplatypus
text:
Call this before anything starts the engine - straight after library(rplatypus) - and before the first call that needs Python.



platypus_use_torch(build = c("pascal", "default"))







build


“pascal” for the last PyTorch built against CUDA 12, or NULL for the default.






There is one reason to: a GeForce GTX 10-series card, or anything older. PyTorch 2.8 and later ship CUDA 13 builds, and CUDA 13 dropped the Maxwell, Pascal and Volta generations outright. No driver update brings them back. Without this, such a card is simply not used and everything runs on the processor, perhaps ten times slower, with nothing obviously wrong.
On anything from Turing - the RTX 20-series onwards - the default is correct and this is unnecessary.



The requirement string now in force, invisibly.



What this prints is a property of the machine it runs on, so an example output here would describe whichever machine built this page rather than yours. Run it and read your own.




library("rplatypus")

library(rplatypus)
platypus_use_torch("pascal")   # GTX 10-series and older

title: rplatypus
text:
A model’s decode is a list of these, not one: several decodings share one forward pass, so a second one costs seconds where a second training run costs an hour. evaluate() then returns a row per model and decoding.



decode_connected_components(minimum_area = NULL)

decode_nearest_seed(minimum_area = NULL)

decode_watershed(minimum_area = NULL)

decode_follow_flows(steps = NULL, step_size = NULL, minimum_area = NULL)







minimum_area


Drop an object smaller than this many pixels. Unset keeps everything, and that is the engine’s default on purpose: the right floor is a property of the data rather than of the method. A nucleus at 256x256 in the Data Science Bowl runs from 4 pixels up, so a floor picked here would silently delete the smallest real objects in one dataset while letting speckle through in another. It is applied after the objects are formed, so it removes answers rather than changing how they were reached.




steps


For decode_follow_flows(), how many Euler steps each pixel takes. Measured as not mattering: one step scores 0.9914 against 0.9923 converged, a span below the 0.0013 two runs differ by, because the field is continuous within an object and diverges at a seam - so the gap between two objects opens on the first step rather than after many. Adjustable because that argument is about this data’s object sizes.




step_size


For decode_follow_flows(), how far one step moves, in pixels, on a unit-length field. A cliff rather than a speed knob: 0.9923 at 1, 0.4715 at 2, 0.0303 at 10. A step longer than a pixel jumps over the sink it was converging on and lands in a neighbour’s basin.






Each declares which separation it can read, and asking for one that cannot read the model’s signal is refused when the specification is built rather than at the end of a run. decode_connected_components() reads none of them - it ignores the separation signal entirely - which is exactly why it belongs in every model’s list: it is the row the signal’s own row has to be read against. Left unset, a model decodes with its own signal’s decoding plus that yardstick.



A decoding block, to be passed inside a model’s decode list.



separations, instance_data()




library("rplatypus")

list(decode_nearest_seed(), decode_connected_components())

[[1]]
[[1]]$name
[1] "nearest_seed"


[[2]]
[[2]]$name
[1] "connected_components"

decode_follow_flows(step_size = 0.5)

$name
[1] "follow_flows"

$step_size
[1] 0.5

title: rplatypus
text:
How the weights are updated. optimizer_adam() unless there is a reason not to: it adapts the step per parameter, so it usually trains without anything tuned except learning_rate. optimizer_sgd() with momentum is the recipe most of the classification literature’s best numbers were produced with, in exchange for depending on a tuned rate and usually a schedule - see callbacks for those.



optimizer_adam(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  beta_1 = 0.9,
  beta_2 = 0.999,
  eps = 1e-08,
  weight_decay = 0,
  amsgrad = FALSE
)

optimizer_adamw(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  beta_1 = 0.9,
  beta_2 = 0.999,
  eps = 1e-08,
  weight_decay = 0.01
)

optimizer_sgd(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  momentum = 0,
  nesterov = FALSE,
  weight_decay = 0
)

optimizer_rmsprop(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  alpha = 0.99,
  momentum = 0,
  eps = 1e-08,
  weight_decay = 0
)

optimizer_adagrad(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  lr_decay = 0,
  eps = 1e-10,
  weight_decay = 0
)

optimizer_adadelta(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  rho = 0.9,
  eps = 1e-06,
  weight_decay = 0
)

optimizer_adamax(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  beta_1 = 0.9,
  beta_2 = 0.999,
  eps = 1e-08,
  weight_decay = 0
)

optimizer_nadam(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  beta_1 = 0.9,
  beta_2 = 0.999,
  eps = 1e-08,
  weight_decay = 0
)







learning_rate


How big a step to take. The one setting worth trying first when a run will not learn: too high and the loss moves without improving, too low and it improves too slowly to tell from not improving at all. Each parameter group decays from its own rate, so an encoder_learning_rate is not flattened by a schedule.




beta_1


Decay for the running average of the gradient. Lower reacts to the last few batches, higher smooths over more of them; 0.9 is the usual value and rarely worth moving.




beta_2


Decay for the running average of the squared gradient, which is what scales each parameter’s step. Below about 0.99 training gets noticeably noisier. In optimizer_adamax() it decays the largest gradient seen instead.




eps


Added to the denominator so a parameter whose gradient has been zero for a while does not take an enormous step. A guard, not a knob.




weight_decay


Pull the weights towards zero at every step, which is L2 regularisation. Off by default because it interacts with the loss and is not free: on a small dataset it can cost more than the overfitting it prevents. In optimizer_adamw() it is applied to the weights directly rather than through the gradient, which is the whole difference between the two.




amsgrad


Keep the largest squared-gradient average seen so far rather than the current one, so the step size never grows back. It fixes a convergence case in Adam’s proof and usually changes nothing in practice; worth trying if a run plateaus and then gets worse.




momentum


Carry a fraction of the previous step into this one. 0 is plain gradient descent; 0.9 is the usual choice and is what makes SGD competitive with the adaptive methods.




nesterov


Look ahead to where momentum is about to carry the weights before measuring the gradient. Needs momentum above 0, and giving it without momentum is refused rather than ignored.




alpha


For optimizer_rmsprop(), the decay for its running average of the squared gradient - the same work beta_2 does in the Adam family, under that family’s name.




lr_decay


For optimizer_adagrad(), shrink the rate further as training goes on, on top of the shrinking Adagrad already does by accumulating every squared gradient it has seen.




rho


For optimizer_adadelta(), how long a window of squared gradients to remember. Adadelta exists to avoid Adagrad’s ever-shrinking step and this is the parameter that does it.






No run in this project has compared them on segmentation, so this page says what each one does differently rather than which is better. available_optimizers() lists them with the arguments each accepts.
The rest are here because a configuration should be able to name what torch offers. optimizer_adamw() is Adam with weight decay applied to the weights rather than through the gradient, which is why its decay defaults to 0.01 rather than 0 - choosing it and leaving the decay at zero leaves nothing to choose. optimizer_adagrad() accumulates every squared gradient it has seen, so its step only ever shrinks and a long run can stop learning; optimizer_adadelta() is the same idea with a window instead of a sum. optimizer_adamax() tracks the largest gradient rather than the average of their squares, which is steadier where a few batches carry very large ones. optimizer_rmsprop() is Adam’s denominator without its momentum, and optimizer_nadam() is Adam with the look-ahead that SGD calls nesterov.
Every argument left unset is decided by the engine, which is where the defaults live.



An optimiser specification.



available_optimizers() for the same list with its arguments, and callbacks() for moving the rate during a run.




library("rplatypus")

optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 1e-4)

$name
[1] "adam"

$learning_rate
[1] 1e-04

$beta_1
[1] 0.9

$beta_2
[1] 0.999

$eps
[1] 1e-08

$weight_decay
[1] 0

$amsgrad
[1] FALSE

optimizer_sgd(learning_rate = 0.01, momentum = 0.9, nesterov = TRUE)

$name
[1] "sgd"

$learning_rate
[1] 0.01

$momentum
[1] 0.9

$nesterov
[1] TRUE

$weight_decay
[1] 0

title: rplatypus
text:
Writes safetensors plus a .json sidecar recording what the weights are for: architecture, input shape, channels, classes, and whatever else you pass. Loading refuses a model they do not belong to, which is what the sidecar is for - weights trained on a different colormap with the same number of classes load cleanly and predict nonsense.



export_weights(object, path, model = NULL, ...)







object


A platypus_fit().




path


Where to write, with or without the .safetensors extension.




model


Which model, by the name in the specification. Defaults to the first.




…


Extra fields for the sidecar, for instance data = “BBBC038v1”, licence = “CC0 1.0”.






Anything in … joins the sidecar. The data they were trained on and its licence belong there: weights whose provenance lives in somebody’s memory cannot be used by anybody else, including you in a year.



The path written, invisibly, with the sidecar’s contents attached as the recorded attribute - so you can see what was put beside the weights without opening the file.




library("rplatypus")

export_weights(fit, "weights/my-run",
             data = "our 2026 cohort", licence = "internal use only")

title: rplatypus
text:
The Data Science Bowl stores one file per nucleus; datasets like it are common. Later masks win where they overlap, so an explicit class beats the background it sits on.



unite_masks(masks)







masks


A list of height x width matrices of class indices.






One height x width matrix.




library("rplatypus")

# Data Science Bowl stores one file per nucleus, so a sample's mask arrives as several
# matrices that have to become one. Later masks win where they overlap.
one <- matrix(1L, 8, 8); one[2:4, 2:4] <- 2L

text:
Predict masks



## S3 method for class 'platypus_fit'
predict(
  object,
  model = NULL,
  split = "test",
  type = c("class", "probability", "channels"),
  space = c("model", "source"),
  cases = NULL,
  each = NULL,
  decode = NULL,
  ...
)







object


A platypus_fit().




model


Which model, by the name given in the specification. Defaults to the first one trained.




split


Which data to predict on.




type


“class” gives the class index per pixel, which is the mask to look at; “probability” keeps the per-class channel. “channels” is for an instance model only and means the model’s own output before any decoding: the class channels are probabilities and a flow field’s components are raw, which is why they are not called probabilities here - a softmax across a flow component and a class returns a number that means nothing. Read them with flow_to_colours().
On an instance fit, “class” is a label map of objects, numbered from 1, and “probability” is refused by name for the reason above.
With regions - overlapping classes - “class” is refused rather than computed. The channels are independent binary questions and do not compete, so the most likely one is not an answer: a pixel may be in three classes and naming one of them drops the rest with nothing in the result to say so. Ask for “probability” and write it with save_class_masks().




space


“model” or “source”; see above. Note that the two return different shapes of thing, an array and a list, because they are different things.




cases


Case names to predict, as evaluate_cases() reports them. With this the result is a named list of just those, in the order asked for. A name that is not in the split is an error rather than a missing entry.




each


A function called as each(case, mask) once per image, instead of the predictions being returned together. Whatever it returns is collected under the case’s name; return NULL from it and nothing accumulates. This is the form that does not need the split to fit in memory.




decode


Which decoding turns the predicted channels into objects, by the name used in the model’s decode list. Unset takes the model’s first, which is the engine’s own default rather than one restated here. Instance models only; for anything else it is refused, because a semantic or detection fit decodes nothing.




…


Unused.






With space = “model”: for “class”, an integer array of image x height x width, classes numbered from 1 to match the colormap; for “probability”, the same with a trailing class axis. Tiled models return images at their original size, reassembled.
With space = “source”: a list of such arrays, one per scan, each on that scan’s grid.
On an instance fit: a list of integer label maps named by case, objects numbered from 1 and 0 for background, one entry per image. A list rather than an array for the reason the detection one is a list, and named rather than ordered because a list paired against case names by position is one dropped batch away from naming the wrong picture. Draw them with overlay_instances() and measure them with instance_sizes().



space = “model” returns everything on the grid the model worked at, stacked into one array. That is what training saw, and it is the only form that can be a single array, because a stack needs one shape.
space = “source” maps each prediction back onto the grid of the scan it was computed from - undoing the resampling and the crop - and therefore returns a list, one mask per scan. This is what you want for anything that has to meet the original data: laying a mask over the scan in a viewer, writing it beside the scan with save_volumes(), or measuring it in millilitres of the scan’s own voxels. Scans differ in size, so the list is not a limitation being worked around - resizing them to a common shape is exactly how a mask ends up describing anatomy it was not computed from.
Two things are lost mapping back, and neither can be recovered. Interpolation softens a boundary, so the mask returns slightly smoother than the model drew it. And where reading cropped anatomy away, the mask comes back padded with background - which means not examined, not nothing there. Give the model an input_shape that covers the anatomy if that distinction matters.



The default returns everything together, which for a tiled run is the whole split at full resolution: 200 fundus photographs at 2048 x 2048 is about 6.7 GB before anything is drawn, and the engine’s own predict was killed by exactly that. Two arguments avoid it.
cases names the ones wanted. each hands them over one at a time and keeps only what the function gives back. They compose: cases says which, each says what to do with them.
The saving is in memory and not in time. The engine’s stream is sequential, so asking for two cases out of two hundred still runs the model over two hundred - it simply never holds more than one answer at once.




library("rplatypus")

masks <- predict(fit, "unet")                     # an array, on the model's grid
masks <- predict(fit, "unet", space = "source")   # a list, on each scan's own grid

# The two worst cases, without holding the other 198.
cases <- evaluate_cases(fit, split = "validation")
worst <- cases$case[order(cases$dice)][1:2]
two <- predict(fit, split = "validation", cases = worst)

# Or walk the split, keeping one number per image and none of the masks.
coverage <- predict(fit, split = "validation", each = function(case, mask) mean(mask > 1))

# `space = "source"` returns a list and not an array, which is the API being
# honest: scans differ in size, a stacked array needs one shape, and resizing
# them to match is how a mask ends up describing anatomy it was not computed from.

text:
The inverse of classes_to_colours(). Anything matching no colour becomes background, and coverage in the result says how much of the mask that was - a number near 1 means the colormap does not describe this dataset, which is the quietest way to train on nothing.



colours_to_classes(mask, colormap, tolerance = 0)







mask


An RGB array: height x width x 3, or with a leading image axis.




colormap


A list of RGB triples, one per class.




tolerance


Allow this much difference per channel. Useful after lossy resizing, though masks should be resized with nearest = TRUE so it is not needed.






A list with classes (indices counted from 1) and coverage (the fraction of pixels that matched a colour).




library("rplatypus")

coloured <- classes_to_colours(matrix(c(1, 2, 2, 1), nrow = 2), binary_colormap)
colours_to_classes(coloured, binary_colormap)$classes

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    1    2
[2,]    2    1

title: rplatypus
text:
Masks come two ways, and this reads both. colormap is for masks stored as pictures, one colour per class. labels is for masks stored as label maps - a vector of the voxel values, in class order - which is how volume formats store them.



read_masks(paths, colormap = NULL, labels = NULL, size = NULL, tolerance = 0)







paths


Image files.




colormap


A list of RGB triples, one per class. Give this or labels.




labels


The voxel value of each class, in class order: c(0, 1) for a binary segmentation. For NIfTI and other label maps. Give this or colormap.




size


c(height, width) to read at, or NULL to keep each image’s own size - which only works if they all agree.




tolerance


Passed to colours_to_classes(). Ignored for label maps, which are compared to within half a unit - a label map that has been resampled or merely passed through a float will not satisfy an exact comparison, and a label that fails to match becomes background.






An array of class indices, counted from 1.




library("rplatypus")

# Masks stored as pictures: the colormap says which colour is which class.
truth <- read_masks(list.files("masks/", full.names = TRUE),
                    colormap = list(c(0, 0, 0), c(255, 255, 255)))

# Masks stored as label maps, which is how volumes do it. Exactly one of the two.
truth <- read_masks("case_01/seg.nii.gz", labels = c(0, 1))

# `tolerance` is for masks that have been through a lossy resize, where a colour
# that should be (255, 0, 0) arrives as (254, 1, 0) and matches nothing.
truth <- read_masks(paths, colormap = voc_colormap, tolerance = 2)

title: rplatypus
text:
The objective the model is trained against. Every one of these works unchanged on volumes as well as images.



loss_iou(smooth = 1)

loss_dice(smooth = 1)

loss_generalized_dice(smooth = 1)

loss_cce(label_smoothing = 0)

loss_cce_dice(cce_weight = 0.5, smooth = 1)

loss_focal(gamma = 2, alpha = NULL)

loss_tversky(alpha = 0.5, smooth = 1)

loss_focal_tversky(alpha = 0.5, gamma = 1, smooth = 1)

loss_combo(alpha = 0.5, ce_ratio = 0.5)

loss_mse(where = NULL)

loss_l1(where = NULL)

loss_smooth_l1(beta = NULL, where = NULL)

loss_lovasz(per_image = FALSE)







smooth


Added to numerator and denominator to keep an empty class finite.




label_smoothing


For cross-entropy, train towards 1 - label_smoothing instead of towards 1, so the model is not pushed to be certain. Worth having where the labels themselves are uncertain, which on a hand-drawn boundary they are.




cce_weight


For loss_cce_dice(), how much of the total the cross-entropy half provides. At 0 or 1 it is one of the two alone, which is worth knowing before tuning it as though it were a third thing.




gamma


For focal losses, how hard to discount the pixels already classified well.




alpha


For Tversky, the weight on false negatives; raising it buys recall. Note that alpha = 0.5 is Dice exactly only when smooth = 0.




ce_ratio


For loss_combo(), how its cross-entropy half is tilted between punishing missed foreground (towards 1) and false alarms (towards 0), while alpha sets how much of the total each half provides.




where


For the three regression losses, where the target means anything and so where the error is averaged. A flow field is defined on the objects and undefined off them - there is no direction towards a centre for a pixel in no object - so the builder writes zero on the background, and “everywhere” would spend most of the objective learning that zero. The foreground is 13.97% of a Data Science Bowl image, so “everywhere” gives 86% of the gradient to a constant; “foreground” is the default for that reason rather than by taste.




beta


For loss_smooth_l1(), where the quadratic part ends and the linear one begins, in the target’s own units. A flow field is scaled to roughly [-1, 1], so the default of 1 makes the whole range quadratic - which is loss_mse() with extra steps. Lower it to get any of the robustness this loss is for.




per_image


For loss_lovasz(), sort the errors of each image separately rather than over the whole batch. The harsher reading, and on mostly empty images the noisier one.






There is one documented separately because it needs a page of its own: loss_boundary() adds the signed distance to the truth’s boundary on top of any of these, which removes the systematic volume bias at some cost in per-case accuracy.
Three of these score numbers rather than classes - loss_mse(), loss_l1() and loss_smooth_l1() - and they are not alternatives to the others. A class target has nothing for them to measure and a continuous one has nothing for an overlap to measure, so they belong in exactly one place: the loss of separation_flows(), where the target is a vector field. Measured against the pinned engine rather than assumed: giving one as any segmentation model’s own loss is refused by name - semantic or instance - and giving a class loss to separation_flows() is refused by name the other way round.
One of these weights the classes rather than treating them alike - loss_generalized_dice(), by the inverse square of how much of the picture each class occupies - and the argument usually made for it is not the argument for it here. It is introduced in the literature as a fix for Dice being dominated by the background, and loss_dice() in this package is a mean over the class channels: a lesion in 1% of the frame already carries the same weight as the 99% around it. Measured on a 1% target, with one prediction that finds the lesion and leaks a false positive of equal size and one that misses it and gets the background perfect:



loss


finds it


misses it


prefers finding by




loss_dice()


0.1658


0.4731


0.3073




loss_cce()


0.1600


0.1600


nothing at all




loss_cce_dice()


0.1629


0.3166


0.1536




loss_generalized_dice()


0.3278


0.9511


0.6233



So what it adds is weight beyond an equal share - on that target the classes come out weighted 1 to 9801 - and the objective that is genuinely dominated is the per-pixel half of loss_cce_dice(): to cross-entropy a false positive and a missed lesion of the same size are the same number of wrong pixels, which is the indifference in that row. Two things follow. With every class the same size this is exactly loss_dice() pooled over the classes, so on a balanced problem it costs nothing and buys nothing. And it is not a third loss_tversky(): Tversky moves the balance between false positives and false negatives by a number you choose, loss_focal_tversky() reweights the hard pixels, and this reweights classes by how much of the image they occupy, computed from each batch rather than set by hand - so a batch holding no lesion at all is scored on flat weights, which is an argument for a larger batch_size on a sparse dataset rather than against the loss.
This page said an instance model’s own until the pin moved to 0.8.0a22, and it was true rather than wrong: the refusal lived on the instance class alone, and a semantic model accepted loss_mse() and trained with it, reporting a validation loss of 0.0014 for a mask that was half missing where loss_cce() reaches a Dice of 1.0000. The default where = “foreground” is what made it look as though it had worked - it evaluates the objective only inside the labelled objects and leaves the background unconstrained. The engine refuses it at either task now (pyplatypus#223).



A loss specification, to be passed to a model constructor.



separation_flows(), whose loss is the one place the regression losses belong




library("rplatypus")

loss_focal(gamma = 2)

$name
[1] "focal"

$gamma
[1] 2

$alpha
NULL

loss_tversky(alpha = 0.7)

$name
[1] "tversky"

$alpha
[1] 0.7

$smooth
[1] 1

loss_smooth_l1(beta = 0.1, where = "foreground")

$name
[1] "smooth_l1"

$beta
[1] 0.1

$where
[1] "foreground"

Two things follow. With every class the same size this is exactly loss_dice() pooled over the classes, so on a balanced problem it costs nothing and buys nothing. And it is not a third loss_tversky(): Tversky moves the balance between false positives and false negatives by a number you choose, loss_focal_tversky() reweights the hard pixels, and this reweights classes by how much of the image they occupy, computed from each batch rather than set by hand - so a batch holding no lesion at all is scored on flat weights, which is an argument for a larger batch_size on a sparse dataset rather than against the loss.
This page said an instance model’s own until the pin moved to 0.8.0a22, and it was true rather than wrong: the refusal lived on the instance class alone, and a semantic model accepted loss_mse() and trained with it, reporting a validation loss of 0.0014 for a mask that was half missing where loss_cce() reaches a Dice of 1.0000. The default where = “foreground” is what made it look as though it had worked - it evaluates the objective only inside the labelled objects and leaves the background unconstrained. The engine refuses it at either task now (pyplatypus#223).
