title: rplatypus
text:
A detector that knows three classes, followed by a classifier that knows eighty: find the objects, cut them out, hand the pieces to something else. predict() returns boxes in each image’s own pixels precisely so they can be used on the photograph they came from, and this is what uses them.



detection_crops(
  object,
  model = NULL,
  split = "test",
  score_threshold = NULL,
  context = 0,
  size = NULL,
  fit = "letterbox",
  ...
)







object


A platypus_fit() from a detection specification.




model


Which model, if the fit holds several.




split


Which split’s images to read.




score_threshold


Crop at this confidence instead of the specification’s operating_point.




context


Expand every box by this fraction of its own width and height, per side.




size


c(height, width) every crop is brought to, or NULL to keep each as cut. Crops of one image differ in size otherwise, which is why this returns a list either way.




fit


“letterbox” to preserve the aspect by padding, “stretch” to fill the frame.




…


Unused.






Cut from the image at its native size, not from the square the network sees. Cropping the letterboxed frame would cut a shrunken object and then scale it back up: on a 1024-wide photograph fed to a 416 model, every crop would be two fifths of the size the data allows.
Four more decisions, each of which taken the other way changes what a downstream model sees without changing anything you would notice:


Rounded outward, so the crop contains the whole box. Rounding to nearest loses up to a pixel per side, which on a 26-pixel platelet is a twelfth of the object.


context grows with the box, not by a number of pixels, so one value suits a platelet and a white cell. Zero by default: a detector’s box is tight by construction, and a classifier trained on whole objects does worse on something cut exactly at the edge - but expanding silently would put things nobody asked for into every crop.


size letterboxes rather than stretches. Resizing a tall box to a square changes the aspect of every non-square object, and a classifier then sees a shape that does not occur in nature. fit = “stretch” is there for models trained that way, and has to be asked for.


Read at operating_point, not at the specification’s score_threshold. That one sits near zero so that average precision integrates the whole ranking - hundreds of boxes an image, almost all of them the tail it exists to measure over. Cropping those would hand a classifier mostly noise.


dropped is the number of boxes that clipped to nothing. A model may place a box off the frame and predict() reports what it said, so at a low threshold some arrive with no extent at all; those are dropped and counted rather than the arrays quietly coming back shorter than the detections.



A list with one entry per image, each a list of key, crops (a list of height x width x channels arrays), boxes, scores, labels, names and dropped.




library("rplatypus")

found <- detection_crops(fit, size = c(224, 224))
length(found[[1]]$crops)
plot_masks(found[[1]]$crops[[1]])        # look at one

# Everything above the operating point, as one flat list ready for another model.
pieces <- unlist(lapply(found, `[[`, "crops"), recursive = FALSE)

title: rplatypus
text:
Trains every model the specification asks for, in order, each with its own data pipeline - so two models may differ in input size or tiling and still be compared fairly, on the same data.



platypus_fit(
  spec,
  device = NULL,
  num_workers = "auto",
  strict_data = TRUE,
  check_masks = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)







spec


A platypus_spec().




device


“cuda”, “cpu”, or NULL to use a GPU when one is present.




num_workers


Processes used to read and decode images. “auto” picks a small number based on the machine. This matters more than it sounds: reading in the main process alone leaves the GPU waiting on the disk, and on the Data Science Bowl at 128x128 that is the difference between 35 seconds an epoch and under 10. Set 0 to avoid multiprocessing entirely if it causes trouble.




strict_data


Treat an incomplete sample as an error. Set FALSE to train on the rest and be told what was skipped.




check_masks


Read a sample of the training masks before training, and refuse when a class the specification declares appears in none of them. A colormap or set of labels that matches none of the labelled tissue is the quietest way a run wastes a day: every mask reads as background, the loss falls because background is most of a medical image, and the model learns to answer "nothing here". Set FALSE only when the missing class is real but rarer than the sample - and see inspect_masks() first, which asks the same question over as much of the data as you like.




verbose


Report each epoch as it finishes.






Validation data is never augmented. Measuring a model on distorted images measures the distortion.
This blocks until training finishes. With verbose = TRUE each epoch is reported as it completes, which on anything longer than a few minutes is the difference between waiting and wondering.



A platypus_fit.




library("rplatypus")

fit <- platypus_fit(spec, verbose = TRUE)
evaluate(fit)
masks <- predict(fit, "unet")

title: rplatypus
text:
The detection counterpart of segmentation_data(). Two layouts, the same two as segmentation: nested_dirs expects one directory per sample holding an images and an annotations subdirectory, and config_file expects a CSV with images and annotations columns. A detection dataset in Pascal VOC’s own layout - one flat JPEGImages beside one flat Annotations - is neither, and the way in is to write three CSV files listing the pairs; examples/detect_blood_cells.py in the engine does exactly that for BCCD in a dozen lines.



detection_data(
  train,
  validation = NULL,
  classes,
  test = NULL,
  split = NULL,
  mode = c("nested_dirs", "config_file"),
  annotation_format = c("pascal_voc", "labelme"),
  coordinates = NULL,
  strict_labels = TRUE,
  window = NULL,
  subdirs = c("images", "annotations"),
  column_sep = ";",
  shuffle = TRUE
)







train, validation


Paths to the training and validation data.




classes


Class names, in class order. Position is the class index the model learns, and that is why it is written down rather than read from the files: sorted, BCCD’s three come out Platelets, RBC, WBC, which is reproducible and anatomically meaningless. A model trained with RBC first and used where the first class is WBC reports plausible boxes with plausible scores and nothing downstream can tell.
There is no background entry, unlike a segmentation colormap. A pixel always belongs to some class, so segmentation needs a name for "none of them"; a region of an image holding no object is simply not a box. One class is therefore a legitimate thing to ask for.




test


Optional test data. Annotations are read if they are there, and the split is then scoreable; without them it can be predicted and evaluate() refuses it by name, because scoring against empty truth would report zero and a zero in a table reads as a result.




split


Divide train instead of naming a validation set: a list with fractions (two numbers, or three to cut a test set too) and group_by, which is required and may be NULL. Exactly one of split and validation.
This is the only way to divide one folder for detection. split_dataset() writes a masks column and so cannot be used here; split divides the samples themselves, so column names never come into it. A test set cut this way carries its annotations, so unlike a separate test folder it can be scored and not only predicted on.




mode


“nested_dirs” or “config_file”.




annotation_format


“pascal_voc” for the XML most detection datasets ship, or “labelme” for its JSON.




coordinates


How to read a Pascal VOC box. The format’s own convention is 1-based and inclusive of both ends, so a ten-pixel-wide box runs xmin=1 xmax=10 and the width is xmax - xmin + 1. Plenty of tools write the same files 0-based and exclusive, where that box is xmin=0 xmax=10. Reading one as the other shifts every box by a pixel and shrinks it by one, which is invisible at a glance and costs real overlap on a small object - at 24 pixels a side, one pixel is 4%.
NULL, the default, means the VOC convention. Only meaningful for pascal_voc: LabelMe stores continuous pixel coordinates and has no convention to pick, so giving both is an error rather than a setting that does nothing.




strict_labels


Refuse an object whose class is not in classes. FALSE skips it instead, which is how you train on two of a dataset’s three classes. TRUE by default, because an unexpected label is more often a typo in classes than an intention.




window


How values in real units reach the model, for DICOM and NIfTI. See segmentation_data(); ignored for ordinary pictures, which is what most detection data is.




subdirs


For nested_dirs, the names of the image and annotation subdirectories.




column_sep


For config_file, what separates several paths in one cell.




shuffle


Shuffle the training data between epochs.






A data specification, to be passed to platypus_spec().



yolo3(), plot_boxes()




library("rplatypus")

detection_data("train/", "valid/", classes = c("RBC", "WBC", "Platelets"))

$validation_path

title: rplatypus
text:
One colour per object, chosen so that no two touching objects share one. The rule is adjacency rather than identity: a colour repeats across the picture and never between neighbours, because nobody reads object 214 by its colour and everybody needs to see where one object ends.



overlay_instances(
  image,
  labels,
  alpha = drawing_style()\$overlay_alpha,
  outline = FALSE,
  colours = drawing_style()\$class_colours
)







image


One image: height x width x 3, height x width x 1 or a matrix. Values may be 0-1 or 0-255.




labels


An instance label map - one integer per object, 0 for background. Not a one-hot array: an object identity cannot be carried by a channel.




alpha


How much of the tint shows. Ignored when outline is true, where the stroke is drawn at full strength, because a translucent outline is a smudge.




outline


Draw one stroke per object instead of filling it, which leaves the tissue entirely visible and is what a pathologist is used to.




colours


The palette to take slots from. Eight by default, mirrored from the engine’s own. A picture needing more colours than this has warns, naming how many it needs and how many objects lost the guarantee: the slot wraps onto a colour a neighbour already holds - provably, since it is only past the end once every colour before it was taken by a neighbour - so two touching objects are drawn as one and this figure answers its own question wrongly. The engine warns in the same words, which is checked rather than claimed. Unreachable on anything measured: the hardest of 670 Data Science Bowl cases needs three of the eight.






That is an exact graph colouring, and it is affordable rather than clever. Measured over all 670 Data Science Bowl cases: the hardest needs three colours and class_colours has eight, while the cheap alternative - colour by object number, modulo the palette - draws one touching pair in ten as a single object.
Eight-connected, so two objects meeting at a corner get different colours. A label-maker goes the other way and joins only along edges, because there the risk is merging two objects into one; here the risk is drawing two as one, which is the opposite direction.



A height x width x 3 array of integers, 0-255.



overlay_instance_agreement() for whether the objects are the right ones, overlay_mask() for classes rather than objects.




library("rplatypus")

image <- array(0.5, dim = c(5, 9, 3))
labels <- matrix(0L, nrow = 5, ncol = 9)
labels[2:4, 2:4] <- 1L
labels[2:4, 5:7] <- 2L   # touching object 1 along a seam
shown <- overlay_instances(image, labels)
# Two touching objects, two colours.
!identical(shown[3, 2, ], shown[3, 6, ])

[1] TRUE

title: rplatypus
text:
The picture the 2020 package drew, and the one no summary statistic replaces. Every annotated box is a point - its width against its height, both as fractions of the model’s input - coloured by class, with the anchors on top.



plot_anchors(object, model = NULL, split = "train", log = FALSE, size = 1.1)







object


A fit from platypus_fit() on a detection specification.




model


Which model, when the specification trained several.




split


Which split’s boxes to draw.




log


Draw both axes on a log scale. Detection datasets span a wide range of sizes


a BCCD platelet is about two fifths the side of a red cell and a fifth of a white one - and on linear axes the smallest class collapses into the corner.






size


Point size for the boxes.






What it answers that a mean overlap does not: whether a class has any anchor near it at all. A mean of 0.65 can be one class covered well and another not covered at all, and those two situations want different fixes. On blood cells the three classes occupy three distinct regions - median sides of 133, 69 and 26 pixels at a 416 input - and anchors fitted to all three together cover them at 0.88, 0.85 and 0.83, so fitting to the mixture does not abandon the smallest class. COCO’s nine cover the same three at 0.64, 0.70 and 0.70: evenly worse rather than blind to one, which is the useful thing to know. They are not aimed elsewhere - they span 10 to 373 pixels a side because COCO holds objects of every size, and most of that range describes nothing here.
Worth drawing for a split the anchors were not fitted on. Anchors that sit among the training boxes and away from the validation ones say the two halves hold different objects, and no training curve shows that.



A ggplot object.



detection_anchors() for the numbers, yolo3() for choosing them.




library("rplatypus")

fit <- platypus_fit(spec)
plot_anchors(fit)                      # the split they were fitted to
plot_anchors(fit, split = "validation")  # and one they were not
crumbs: Draw the anchors against the boxes they were fitted to

title: rplatypus
text:
Three colours rather than one: what was found, what was missed, and what was invented. A Dice of 0.85 says nothing about which of the three is costing you, and for most clinical questions they are not interchangeable - a missed lesion and a false alarm are different kinds of wrong.



overlay_agreement(
  image,
  prediction,
  truth,
  alpha = drawing_style()\$overlay_alpha,
  colours = drawing_style()\$agreement_colours
)







image


A height x width x channels array.




prediction, truth


Class indices, counted from 1.




alpha


How strongly to tint.




colours


Named colours for hit, missed and false_alarm.






A height x width x 3 array of 0-255 integers.




library("rplatypus")

image <- array(runif(8 * 8 * 3, 0.2, 0.6), dim = c(8, 8, 3))
truth <- matrix(1L, 8, 8); truth[2:4, 2:4] <- 2L
predicted <- matrix(1L, 8, 8); predicted[3:5, 2:4] <- 2L
shown <- overlay_agreement(image, prediction = predicted, truth = truth)
dim(shown)

[1] 8 8 3

# Three colours, not one: a missed lesion and a false alarm cost different things,
# and a single overlap score hides which one you have.
crumbs: Where a prediction and the truth disagree

title: rplatypus
text:
The volume counterpart of save_class_masks(), and the one regions was motivated by: BraTS names three overlapping regions and stores them as volumes. A label-map NIfTI holds one integer per voxel, so save_volumes() refuses an overlapping prediction rather than reducing it, and this is what it refuses it in favour of - one binary volume per class, each carrying the geometry of the scan it was predicted from.



save_class_volumes(
  masks,
  dir,
  reference,
  classes,
  names = NULL,
  suffix = "",
  threshold = 0.5
)







masks


Channel probabilities - a list of depth x height x width x class arrays, which is what predict(type = “probability”, space = “source”) gives, or one stacked volume x depth x height x width x class array.




dir


Directory to write into; created if it does not exist.




reference


The scan each mask was predicted from, as paths. Every class of one scan is written with that scan’s geometry, which is the whole reason this is not save_class_masks() with a different extension.




classes


One name per channel, in channel order, which is the order the regions were written in. inspect_masks() names them the same way.




names


File name stems, one per volume. Defaults to the reference file names with their extensions removed - and names that collide are refused, because one directory per case usually means the same filename inside each.




suffix


Added before the class, so predictions from different models can sit in one directory.




threshold


A class is written where its channel reaches this. 0.5 is what every metric in the engine thresholds a channel at.






Each file is <name><suffix>_<class>.nii.gz. The class name becomes part of a filename the same way save_class_masks() does, and two class names that become the same filename are refused rather than written.
Why one file per class rather than one file with several values: a voxel in the tumour core is also in the whole tumour, and no single integer says both. Any viewer can load three binary masks over one scan; none can unpack an overlap out of one label map.



The paths written, invisibly, volume by volume and within a volume class by class.



save_class_masks() for 2D, save_volumes() for exclusive classes.




library("rplatypus")

channels <- predict(fit, "brats", split = "test", type = "probability", space = "source")
save_class_volumes(channels, "predictions",
                   reference = split_path(split, "test")$image,
                   classes = c("whole tumour", "tumour core", "enhancing"))
crumbs: Save overlapping classes as one NIfTI per class

title: rplatypus
text:
The detection counterpart of plot_masks(), and the function the 2020 package had under this name. Boxes arrive from predict() in each image’s own pixels, so they land on the picture without anything being undone first.



plot_boxes(
  images,
  boxes,
  truth = NULL,
  which = NULL,
  min_score = drawing_style()\$box_min_score,
  labels = NULL,
  colours = drawing_style()\$box_colours,
  size = 0.6,
  text_size = 3
)







images


An image stack from read_images(), or a single image.




boxes


Boxes to draw: one data frame as predict() returns per image, or a list of them - one per image in images. Columns xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax, and optionally name and score.




truth


Boxes to draw as ground truth, the same shape as boxes.




which


Which images to draw. Defaults to the first four, like plot_masks().




min_score


Drop predicted boxes below this confidence before drawing. The default follows a detector’s own score_threshold of 0.01, which is kept low so average precision can be computed over the whole ranking - and which puts far more boxes on a picture than anyone wants to look at. 0.5 is the usual choice for a figure.




labels


Row labels. Defaults to the names of boxes, which predict() sets to the sample keys.




colours


Named vector giving the colour for prediction and for truth.




size


Line width of a box.




text_size


Size of the class label, or NULL to draw no labels.






Predictions and truth can be drawn together, and when they are, the point is the comparison: truth in one colour, predictions in another, both on the same image. A detector that found the right number of objects in the wrong places and one that found the wrong number in the right places score similarly and look nothing alike.



A ggplot object.



predict.platypus_fit(), plot_masks()




library("rplatypus")

found <- predict(fit, split = "test")
plot_boxes(read_images(files, size = NULL), found, min_score = 0.5)

title: rplatypus
text:
regions gives a channel per named class and a sigmoid per channel, so a pixel may be in several classes at once - that is the point of it. A colour map cannot hold that: one pixel gets one colour. save_masks() therefore refuses such a prediction, and this is what it refuses it in favour of - one binary picture per class, named after the class.



save_class_masks(
  masks,
  dir,
  classes,
  names = NULL,
  suffix = "",
  threshold = 0.5
)







masks


Channel probabilities from predict(fit, type = “probability”) - an image x height x width x class array, or one height x width x class array.
Class indices are the wrong input and are refused where a shape or a value can prove it: any value above 1 is not a probability. What cannot be proved is a stack of class-index masks whose values are all 1 - image x height x width has the same rank as one image’s height x width x class, exactly as save_masks() cannot tell a stack of volumes from a stack of images - so that one is read as one image with eight channels and caught by classes not having eight names.




dir


Directory to write into; created if it does not exist.




classes


One name per channel, in channel order, which is the order the regions were written in and the order every per-class score is reported in. inspect_masks() names them the same way. Called classes and not names because names in this family is the files - see below.




names


File name stems, one per image, or the source image paths to take them from. Defaults to mask_0001 and so on. The engine’s own function calls this cases; in R it is names, matching save_masks() and save_volumes(), and classes carries what the engine calls names.




suffix


Added before the class, so predictions from different models can sit in one directory without overwriting each other.




threshold


A class is written where its channel reaches this. 0.5 is what every metric in the engine thresholds a channel at, so a different number here writes pictures that disagree with the scores printed beside them.






Each file is <name><suffix><class>.png, black and white, so it opens in anything and thresholds back to exactly what was written. A class name becomes a filename by replacing anything outside letters, digits, dot, dash and underscore with , so whole tumour is whole_tumour on disk; two class names that become the same filename are refused rather than written, because one file would hold the second class with the first silently gone.
A class nothing reaches is written as an empty picture rather than skipped. A missing file reads as this run did not produce that class and an empty one as it did and the answer was nothing, which are different findings and only one of them is true.



The paths written, invisibly, image by image and within an image class by class.



save_masks() for exclusive classes as one colour picture, save_volumes() for volumes as NIfTI.




library("rplatypus")

spec <- platypus_spec(... )
channels <- predict(fit, "brats", split = "test", type = "probability")
save_class_masks(channels, "predictions", classes = c("whole tumour", "core", "enhancing"))
crumbs: Write overlapping classes, one file per class

title: rplatypus
text:
Two layouts. nested_dirs expects one directory per sample containing an images and a masks subdirectory - the Data Science Bowl arrangement, where a sample may hold dozens of separate mask files that are combined into one. config_file expects a CSV with images and masks columns, several paths per cell if needed, resolved relative to the file itself so a configuration travels with its data.



segmentation_data(
  train,
  validation = NULL,
  colormap = NULL,
  labels = NULL,
  regions = NULL,
  classes_from = NULL,
  test = NULL,
  split = NULL,
  mode = c("nested_dirs", "config_file"),
  window = NULL,
  dicom_window = NULL,
  target_spacing = NULL,
  channels_from = NULL,
  subdirs = c("images", "masks"),
  column_sep = ";",
  shuffle = TRUE
)







train, validation


Paths to the training and validation data. A split_dataset() may be given as train on its own: it carries all three paths and selects config_file mode, so a split needs no unpacking.
validation = FALSE says this run has no validation set, which is the third and last answer to the question validation and split both answer - a final fit on every case you have, once the hyperparameters are settled. It goes in this argument rather than a new one because it is the same question, and a second argument could contradict the first.
Leaving validation and split both unset is still an error, and that is deliberate: "I have no validation set" and "I forgot" look identical, and only one of them is a decision.




colormap


A list of RGB triples, one per class, background first. For masks stored as pictures. Give this or labels, not both.




labels


The voxel value of each class, in class order, for masks stored as label maps - c(0, 1) for a binary segmentation, c(0, 1, 2) where 1 is liver and 2 is tumour. This is how NIfTI and every other volume format label anything. Give this or colormap, not both.
Include 0 unless the masks really do fill every voxel. A value matching no entry falls back to the first class, so a list without 0 trains the background as whatever that first class is. The engine refuses that combination rather than let it look plausible, which means the error arrives before the run and not in the scores.




regions


Overlapping classes, named as unions of a label-map value set: a list of list(name = , of = ), where of holds the voxel values belonging to that region. list(list(name = “whole tumour”, of = c(1, 2, 4)), list(name = “enhancing”, of = 4)) is the BraTS shape, and the second entry shows that a single value is ordinary rather than an edge case. Give this, colormap or labels, not more than one.
Two things this field changes that its name does not say. There is no background entry, so n_class here is not the same number it would be for that many labels - with labels the background is a class and with regions it is not. And each channel is an independent binary question, a sigmoid per channel rather than one softmax across them, so a voxel may be in several regions at once - which is the whole point, and the reason save_masks() cannot write such a prediction as one picture.
Two regions are the minimum: one region is ordinary binary segmentation, which labels = c(0, 1) already says. Disjoint regions are allowed and mean something - grouping several values into one class and dropping the background channel - so they are not refused.




classes_from


For masks kept as one binary file per class: one pattern per class, in class order. The fourth way of saying what a mask’s classes are, and the only one that can express an overlap that was drawn independently - a vessel crossing an organ, or two annotators’ masks of the same structure. Give this, colormap, labels or regions, not more than one.
It is regions’ sibling, not its replacement, and the difference is the file on disk. regions derives overlapping channels from the values of one label map, which is how BraTS stores its ground truth; this reads channels that were separate files to begin with, because no single voxel value can hold two things drawn independently. Everything the two share is everything after the target: no background entry, a sigmoid per channel rather than one softmax across them, a voxel that may be in several classes at once, and a prediction save_masks() cannot write as one picture - use save_class_masks() or save_class_volumes().
Patterns are Python regular expressions matched against a sample’s mask files, with the same two rules channels_from has for images and for the same reason: each must match exactly one file, and every mask file must be claimed by some pattern. Both halves are refused, because each is invisible from the other side - a pattern matching nothing is a class the model is never shown, and a file matching no pattern is a class the data has and nobody asked for. R’s own quoting applies: c(“_vessel\.png$“,”_organ\.png$“).
The order is written rather than inferred, and here it matters more than for channels: a model trained with the vessel in the first channel and used where the first channel is the organ answers plausibly, in range, and nothing further down can notice.




test


Optional test data. Only images are read from it.




split


Divide train instead of naming a validation set: a list with fractions (two numbers, or three to cut a test set as well) and group_by. Exactly one of split, validation, and validation = FALSE.
group_by has to be given, even as NULL. It is a regular expression read against each sample’s name, and everything sharing a group lands in a single split - usually a patient, sometimes a study or a scanner. NULL divides by file instead, and is a perfectly good answer when the images are independent.
It is required rather than optional because the mistake it prevents leaves no trace: slices of one patient in training and validation at once make validation measure memory rather than generalisation, and the score comes out several points too high with nothing in the output to say so.
Nothing is written. split_dataset() is still the way when the three CSV files are the point - to keep, to hand to a colleague, to cite - and its result can be passed straight to train.




mode


“nested_dirs” or “config_file”.




window


How values in real units reach the model. A named window - “lung”, “soft_tissue”, “bone”, “brain”, “abdomen”, “liver”, “mediastinum”, “subdural”, “stroke” - or an explicit c(centre, width) in Hounsfield units, or “auto” for the window the file recorded, which only DICOM has, or “full” for the whole range present. Applies to DICOM and to NIfTI; ignored for ordinary pictures, which are already 0-255.
Worth choosing rather than leaving: a fixed window is what makes two scans comparable. Scaling each scan by its own darkest and brightest voxel lets a single metal implant or marker rescale everything else in it.
NULL, the default, sends nothing and lets the engine decide - which also keeps ordinary image work running against an engine too old to know the setting exists.




dicom_window


The former name of window, still accepted. It was accurate while DICOM was the only format that needed it.




target_spacing


For volumes: resample every scan to this many millimetres per voxel, then centre-crop or pad to the model’s input_shape. Without it a volume is simply resized into that shape, which is only harmless when every scan covers the same amount of the patient - and clinical scans do not. Forty slices of 1 mm is 40 mm of patient and forty of 2.5 mm is 100 mm, so resizing alone leaves the same organ a different size in each, and nothing in the data says so.
c(1, 1, 1) is the usual starting point. Ignored for 2D.




channels_from


For datasets that keep one channel per file: one pattern per channel, in channel order. BraTS ships four MRI sequences per patient - T1, T1 after contrast, T2 and FLAIR - because different tumour structures are visible in different sequences; satellite sets keep their bands apart the same way.
The order is stated rather than inferred, and that is the point. Sorted, the BraTS names come out flair, t1, t1ce, t2 - reproducible and anatomically meaningless. A model trained with FLAIR in channel one and used on data whose channel one is T1 returns a plausible answer with the right shape and the right range, and nothing further down can notice.
Patterns are Python regular expressions, like group_by in split_dataset(), and R’s own quoting applies: c(“_t1\.nii”, “_t1ce\.nii”, “_t2\.nii”, “_flair\.nii”). title: rplatypus
text:
Two layouts. nested_dirs expects one directory per sample containing an images and a masks subdirectory - the Data Science Bowl arrangement, where a sample may hold dozens of separate mask files that are combined into one. config_file expects a CSV with images and masks columns, several paths per cell if needed, resolved relative to the file itself so a configuration travels with its data.



segmentation_data(
  train,
  validation = NULL,
  colormap = NULL,
  labels = NULL,
  regions = NULL,
  classes_from = NULL,
  test = NULL,
  split = NULL,
  mode = c("nested_dirs", "config_file"),
  window = NULL,
  dicom_window = NULL,
  target_spacing = NULL,
  channels_from = NULL,
  subdirs = c("images", "masks"),
  column_sep = ";",
  shuffle = TRUE
)







train, validation


Paths to the training and validation data. A split_dataset() may be given as train on its own: it carries all three paths and selects config_file mode, so a split needs no unpacking.
validation = FALSE says this run has no validation set, which is the third and last answer to the question validation and split both answer - a final fit on every case you have, once the hyperparameters are settled. It goes in this argument rather than a new one because it is the same question, and a second argument could contradict the first.
Leaving validation and split both unset is still an error, and that is deliberate: "I have no validation set" and "I forgot" look identical, and only one of them is a decision.




colormap


A list of RGB triples, one per class, background first. For masks stored as pictures. Give this or labels, not both.




labels


The voxel value of each class, in class order, for masks stored as label maps - c(0, 1) for a binary segmentation, c(0, 1, 2) where 1 is liver and 2 is tumour. This is how NIfTI and every other volume format label anything. Give this or colormap, not both.
Include 0 unless the masks really do fill every voxel. A value matching no entry falls back to the first class, so a list without 0 trains the background as whatever that first class is. The engine refuses that combination rather than let it look plausible, which means the error arrives before the run and not in the scores.




regions


Overlapping classes, named as unions of a label-map value set: a list of list(name = , of = ), where of holds the voxel values belonging to that region. list(list(name = “whole tumour”, of = c(1, 2, 4)), list(name = “enhancing”, of = 4)) is the BraTS shape, and the second entry shows that a single value is ordinary rather than an edge case. Give this, colormap or labels, not more than one.
Two things this field changes that its name does not say. There is no background entry, so n_class here is not the same number it would be for that many labels - with labels the background is a class and with regions it is not. And each channel is an independent binary question, a sigmoid per channel rather than one softmax across them, so a voxel may be in several regions at once - which is the whole point, and the reason save_masks() cannot write such a prediction as one picture.
Two regions are the minimum: one region is ordinary binary segmentation, which labels = c(0, 1) already says. Disjoint regions are allowed and mean something - grouping several values into one class and dropping the background channel - so they are not refused.




classes_from


For masks kept as one binary file per class: one pattern per class, in class order. The fourth way of saying what a mask’s classes are, and the only one that can express an overlap that was drawn independently - a vessel crossing an organ, or two annotators’ masks of the same structure. Give this, colormap, labels or regions, not more than one.
It is regions’ sibling, not its replacement, and the difference is the file on disk. regions derives overlapping channels from the values of one label map, which is how BraTS stores its ground truth; this reads channels that were separate files to begin with, because no single voxel value can hold two things drawn independently. Everything the two share is everything after the target: no background entry, a sigmoid per channel rather than one softmax across them, a voxel that may be in several classes at once, and a prediction save_masks() cannot write as one picture - use save_class_masks() or save_class_volumes().
Patterns are Python regular expressions matched against a sample’s mask files, with the same two rules channels_from has for images and for the same reason: each must match exactly one file, and every mask file must be claimed by some pattern. Both halves are refused, because each is invisible from the other side - a pattern matching nothing is a class the model is never shown, and a file matching no pattern is a class the data has and nobody asked for. R’s own quoting applies: c(“_vessel\.png$“,”_organ\.png$“).
The order is written rather than inferred, and here it matters more than for channels: a model trained with the vessel in the first channel and used where the first channel is the organ answers plausibly, in range, and nothing further down can notice.




test


Optional test data. Only images are read from it.




split


Divide train instead of naming a validation set: a list with fractions (two numbers, or three to cut a test set as well) and group_by. Exactly one of split, validation, and validation = FALSE.
group_by has to be given, even as NULL. It is a regular expression read against each sample’s name, and everything sharing a group lands in a single split - usually a patient, sometimes a study or a scanner. NULL divides by file instead, and is a perfectly good answer when the images are independent.
It is required rather than optional because the mistake it prevents leaves no trace: slices of one patient in training and validation at once make validation measure memory rather than generalisation, and the score comes out several points too high with nothing in the output to say so.
Nothing is written. split_dataset() is still the way when the three CSV files are the point - to keep, to hand to a colleague, to cite - and its result can be passed straight to train.




mode


“nested_dirs” or “config_file”.




window


How values in real units reach the model. A named window - “lung”, “soft_tissue”, “bone”, “brain”, “abdomen”, “liver”, “mediastinum”, “subdural”, “stroke” - or an explicit c(centre, width) in Hounsfield units, or “auto” for the window the file recorded, which only DICOM has, or “full” for the whole range present. Applies to DICOM and to NIfTI; ignored for ordinary pictures, which are already 0-255.
Worth choosing rather than leaving: a fixed window is what makes two scans comparable. Scaling each scan by its own darkest and brightest voxel lets a single metal implant or marker rescale everything else in it.
NULL, the default, sends nothing and lets the engine decide - which also keeps ordinary image work running against an engine too old to know the setting exists.




dicom_window


The former name of window, still accepted. It was accurate while DICOM was the only format that needed it.




target_spacing


For volumes: resample every scan to this many millimetres per voxel, then centre-crop or pad to the model’s input_shape. Without it a volume is simply resized into that shape, which is only harmless when every scan covers the same amount of the patient - and clinical scans do not. Forty slices of 1 mm is 40 mm of patient and forty of 2.5 mm is 100 mm, so resizing alone leaves the same organ a different size in each, and nothing in the data says so.
c(1, 1, 1) is the usual starting point. Ignored for 2D.




channels_from


For datasets that keep one channel per file: one pattern per channel, in channel order. BraTS ships four MRI sequences per patient - T1, T1 after contrast, T2 and FLAIR - because different tumour structures are visible in different sequences; satellite sets keep their bands apart the same way.
The order is stated rather than inferred, and that is the point. Sorted, the BraTS names come out flair, t1, t1ce, t2 - reproducible and anatomically meaningless. For nested_dirs, the names of the image and mask subdirectories.

For config_file, what separates several paths in one cell.

Shuffle the training data between epochs.

title: rplatypus
text:
Predictions are only half useful while they are an array in a session. This writes them as ordinary PNGs that open in anything - ImageJ, QuPath, a viewer, a colleague’s machine - and returns the paths, so it can sit at the end of a pipeline.



save_masks(masks, dir, colormap, names = NULL, suffix = "")







masks


Class indices from predict.platypus_fit() - an image x height x width array, or one height x width matrix. Probabilities are accepted too and reduced to the most likely class.
For volumes use save_volumes(), which writes NIfTI carrying the geometry of the scan each mask came from. This function cannot reliably tell a stack of volumes from a stack of images with a class axis - the ranks are identical - so it does not try; it refuses only the case a shape can prove.
For overlapping classes use save_class_masks(). A prediction where some pixel is in two classes at once is refused here rather than reduced: one pixel gets one colour, so writing it as a colour map would mean choosing one of the classes it is in and leaving nothing in the file to say that happened.




dir


Directory to write into; created if it does not exist.




colormap


A list of RGB triples, one per class.




names


File names, or the source image paths to take names from. Defaults to mask_0001.png and so on.




suffix


Added before the extension, so predictions from different models can sit in one directory without overwriting each other.






Files go where you say, not beside the images they came from. Writing into somebody’s dataset directory is a surprising thing for a function to do, and a second run against a different model would quietly mix its results in with the first.



The paths written, invisibly.




library("rplatypus")

masks <- predict(fit, "unet", split = "test")
save_masks(masks, "predictions", binary_colormap, suffix = "_unet")

title: rplatypus
text:
overlay_agreement() answers the same three-way question about pixels, and on an instance result that is the wrong unit: a merged pair and a split object are both nearly perfect pixelwise and both wrong, which is exactly what an average precision will not tell anybody. This matches whole objects at one IoU threshold, the way the metric matches them, so the picture cannot disagree with the number it illustrates.



overlay_instance_agreement(
  image,
  prediction,
  truth,
  threshold = 0.5,
  alpha = drawing_style()\$overlay_alpha,
  colours = drawing_style()\$agreement_colours
)







image


One image, as overlay_instances() takes it.




prediction


An instance label map from a model.




truth


An instance label map from the annotation.




threshold


The IoU above which a predicted object counts as a true one, strictly greater. 0.5 is the loosest of the challenge’s ten thresholds, so it is the kindest reading, and below 0.5 is refused for the reason the metric refuses it: there one prediction can satisfy two true objects and the match stops being one to one.




alpha


How much of the tint shows.




colours


Named hit, missed and false_alarm, as overlay_agreement() takes them.






A height x width x 3 array of integers, 0-255.



overlay_instances() for the objects themselves.




library("rplatypus")

image <- array(0.5, dim = c(5, 11, 3))
truth <- matrix(0L, nrow = 5, ncol = 11)
truth[2:4, 2:4] <- 1L
truth[2:4, 6:8] <- 2L
predicted <- matrix(0L, nrow = 5, ncol = 11)
predicted[2:4, 2:4] <- 1L    # one found
predicted[2:4, 9:11] <- 2L   # one invented, and object 2 missed
shown <- overlay_instance_agreement(image, predicted, truth)
# Three different colours: hit, missed, invented.
nrow(unique(rbind(shown[3, 2, ], shown[3, 6, ], shown[3, 10, ])))

[1] 3

title: rplatypus
text:
A detector cannot be reloaded without its anchors, and when they were fitted rather than named in the specification this is the only record. export_weights() writes them into the sidecar for the same reason.



detection_anchors(object, model = NULL)







object


A fit from platypus_fit() on a detection specification.




model


Which model, when the specification trained several.






A list: anchors as three groups of pairs, fitted saying whether they were fitted to your data, and when they were, the mean overlap they achieve and a data frame with one row per anchor.




library("rplatypus")

anchors <- detection_anchors(fit)
anchors$mean_iou        # ~0.88 fitted on BCCD, against 0.65 for COCO's nine
anchors$per_anchor      # one row per anchor

# `fitted` says whether these were fitted to the data or taken from the
# specification. A detector cannot be reloaded without them, so they travel
# with the weights.
crumbs: The anchors a detector used, and whether they were fitted

title: rplatypus
text:
One row per model: what it is, how big it is, how long it trained, and how it scored.



evaluate(object, ...)

## S3 method for class 'platypus_fit'
evaluate(object, split = "validation", ...)







object


A platypus_fit().




…


Unused.




split


Which data to score on: “validation”, “train” or “test”.






The loss column is only comparable between models trained on the same loss, which is why loss_function is there beside it. A Focal-Tversky of 0.05 is not better than a CCE-Dice of 0.14; it is not even the same question. Metrics stay comparable, because they measure the mask rather than the objective.



A data frame, one row per model.



evaluate is also exported by the evaluate package, which knitr depends on, so the two mask each other depending on which was attached last. It is a generic here, so evaluate(fit) dispatches on the fit’s class whichever one you reach - and rplatypus::evaluate(fit) says so outright. The name is kept because it is the word for what this does; platypus_fit() carries a prefix only because fit is a generic in the tidymodels packages and a plain fit would have been theirs to own.




library("rplatypus")

evaluate(fit)                      # one row per model, on the validation split
evaluate(fit, split = "test")

# A split with no masks is refused by name rather than scored against nothing;
# `predict()` still works on it.
